Sapphire Sleet npm postinstall dropper: node executing easy-day-js setup.cjs AIInstallation High
Hunts the Mastra supply-chain postinstall hook where npm spawns Node.js to run the easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs --no-warnings) on any workstation or CI/CD runner that ran npm install/update after the poisoned versions. Article-specific because it anchors on the typosquat package name and the exact dropper filename, not generic node execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact dropper filename (setup.cjs), the typosquat package name (easy-day-js) and the executing interpreter (node), all named verbatim in the weaponized package.json and Microsoft's own hunting query (Code Block 1). The combination is high-fidelity; neither string appears in benign node workloads together. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-links-mastra-ai-supply-chain-attack-to-north-korean-hackers/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or malware analysts intentionally detonating easy-day-js in a sandbox VM
  • An internal package legitimately named with 'setup.cjs' as its own postinstall build script (native-addon builds via node-gyp/prebuild-install)
  • EDR/CI test harnesses that replay the IOC for detection validation
  • A developer who pinned the package pre-disclosure and is reproducing the issue for remediation
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "setup.cjs" and not (ProcessCommandLine has "easy-day-js") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp", "prebuild-install"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the FolderPath/working dir resolves to a node_modules/easy-day-js path and check InitiatingProcessCommandLine for npm install/ci. Pull the SHA256 of setup.cjs and compare to the article hashes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner, kill the node process tree, and rotate every credential/token reachable from that environment (npm tokens, cloud keys, CI secrets, SSH keys) since the payload runs with the developer's full context. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (C2 to 23.254.164.92/.123), UC3 (NvmProtocal Run key), UC4 (.pkg_logs marker) and UC5 (second-stage from NodePackages) on the same DeviceId, and sweep package-lock.json across the org for easy-day-js@1.11.22 and @mastra deps published with the v1.13.1-class anomaly.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.cjs", "easy-day-js")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "node"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.cjs", "easy-day-js")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Sapphire Sleet npm postinstall dropper via easy-day-js setup.cjs
id: 6f1a2b3c-4d5e-6f70-8a90-1b2c3d4e5f60
status: experimental
description: Detects Node.js executing the easy-day-js setup.cjs postinstall dropper from the Mastra npm supply chain compromise
references:
    - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
    - attack.t1195.002
    - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\node.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'setup.cjs'
            - 'easy-day-js'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*node.exe OR *Node.exe OR *NODE.EXE) @CommandLine:(*setup.cjs* OR *easy-day-js*)

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") AND (Processes.process="*setup.cjs*" OR Processes.process="*easy-day-js*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Mastra easy-day-js C2 beacon to 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from any host to the two Sapphire Sleet C2 endpoints used by the easy-day-js dropper to fetch the second-stage wallet-stealer/RAT (GET 23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878 and the 23.254.164.123:443 secondary). Article-specific via the hardcoded C2 IPs decoded from the obfuscated string table. Rationale: Both IPs are decoded directly from the dropper's obfuscated string table in the article (23.254.164.92:8000 primary download URL /update/49890878, and 23.254.164.123:443 secondary C2). Hardcoded attacker IPs are the highest-fidelity IOC available; any contact is presumed malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://orca.security/resources/blog/mastra-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox sandboxing the sample and reaching the live C2
  • A SOAR/enrichment connector actively probing the IOC IPs for reachability
  • Vulnerability scanner sweeping the /24 (23.254.164.0/24, Hostwinds hosting range) that happens to touch these IPs
  • Shared NAT egress IP attribution making it hard to identify the true originating host (verify InitiatingProcessFileName is node)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("thor.exe", "nessus.exe", "nuclei.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine for the connection — confirm it is node executing setup.cjs or a NodePackages .js. Note whether the request hit :8000 (payload download) or :443 (secondary C2). 2) CONTAIN: Block 23.254.164.92 and 23.254.164.123 at perimeter/EDR, isolate the host, and capture the on-disk second stage before reimage. 3) HUNT: Correlate the connection time with UC1 (postinstall) and UC5 (detached node) on the same DeviceId; sweep proxy/firewall and DNS for any host in the org that resolved or connected to the Hostwinds C2 range, and rotate all secrets exposed on affected build environments.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js persistence: NvmProtocal Run key / ProgramData NodePackages autostart AIInstallation High
Hunts the Windows persistence the second stage establishes: an HKCU CurrentVersion\Run value named 'NvmProtocal' and/or autostart data pointing at C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\. Article-specific via the exact, attacker-chosen artifact name (a deliberate 'nvm'/'protocol' misspelling) and drop directory from the persistence matrix. Rationale: Uses the persistence matrix verbatim: the artifact name 'NvmProtocal' (an attacker misspelling of nvm/protocol) and the drop directory 'NodePackages'. Both are non-standard and not produced by the legitimate nvm tool, dayjs, or Node itself, making them low-FP autostart anchors. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-iocs-and-response-runbook
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool that coincidentally writes a Run value containing the substring 'NodePackages' (rare)
  • Backup/migration software replaying an old HKCU\Run hive that contains a pre-existing infection artifact
  • Detection-engineering validation that writes the NvmProtocal value into a Run key on a test host
  • Golden-image build that captured a compromised profile (investigate, do not allowlist)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full RegistryValueData to recover the second-stage path (expected C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\<random>.js) and confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is node. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the NvmProtocal Run value, remove the C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\ contents after capturing copies for IR, isolate the host, and rotate the user's credentials/tokens. 3) HUNT: Check macOS (~/Library/NodePackages/com.nvm.protocal.plist LaunchAgent) and Linux (~/.config/systemd/nvmconf/nvmconf.service) equivalents across the fleet, and correlate to UC1/UC2/UC5 on the same host to establish the full chain.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryValueName =~ "NvmProtocal" or RegistryValueData has "NodePackages"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryValue =~ "NvmProtocal" or RegistryValueData has "NodePackages"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js install markers: .pkg_history / .pkg_logs dropped by Node.js AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the dropper's filesystem tracking markers — $TMPDIR/.pkg_history (compromised package install path) and $TMPDIR/.pkg_logs (package name XOR-0x80 encoded) — written by the node process during the postinstall phase. Article-specific via the exact marker filenames written by the Node.js dropper. Rationale: The two marker filenames (.pkg_history, .pkg_logs) are decoded verbatim in the article (the .pkg_logs XOR-0x80 marker resolves to 'easy-day-js'). Scoping the writer to node and the filenames to these two strings makes it a clean, low-volume hunt for any infected install — including ones where C2 was unreachable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1027 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package manager or build tool that writes dotfiles named .pkg_history/.pkg_logs to temp (uncommon; verify the writer is node and the path is the OS temp dir)
  • Forensic tooling restoring the markers during IR replay on a clean host
  • Security validation harness dropping the IOC files for rule testing
  • Backup agents copying the temp dir of a previously infected user profile
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read .pkg_history to recover the install path of the compromised node_modules package, and confirm InitiatingProcessCommandLine shows setup.cjs / npm install. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the node tree, and treat the workstation/runner secrets as exposed — rotate npm/cloud/CI tokens. 3) HUNT: Even if no C2 (UC2) fired, sweep for the persistence artifacts (UC3) and second-stage process (UC5) on the same host, and grep the org's lockfiles for easy-day-js@1.11.22 and @mastra packages republished around the v1.13.1 anomaly window (2026-06-16/17).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ (".pkg_history", ".pkg_logs")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileName in~ (".pkg_history", ".pkg_logs")
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js second stage: detached Node.js executing .js from ProgramData NodePackages AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the second-stage execution where the dropper (node) spawns a fully detached, window-hidden child node process running a randomly named .js written under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\. Article-specific via the node→node parent/child chain plus the unique NodePackages drop directory, surfacing the random script via the command line rather than hardcoding it. Rationale: Anchors on the article's described execution shape (dropper-node spawns a detached hidden node running a randomly named .js) plus the NodePackages drop directory from the persistence matrix. Rather than hardcoding the random filename, it surfaces the full command line so the analyst recovers the script path; node-spawning-node into ProgramData is rare in benign workloads. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://orca.security/resources/blog/mastra-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-links-mastra-ai-supply-chain-attack-to-north-korean-hackers/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Node application installed under C:\ProgramData that uses a child_process to run helper .js scripts (verify the parent is node and the path component is literally NodePackages)
  • Electron/CLI tools bundling their runtime under ProgramData and forking worker scripts
  • Internal build tooling that nests node invocations and references a 'NodePackages' cache directory
  • Developer reproducing the infection chain in a controlled VM
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp", "electron-builder") and FolderPath has "Program Files")

1) TRIAGE: From the matched command line recover the random .js path under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\, hash it, and compare to the article's second-stage SHA256s; confirm the parent node lineage traces back to setup.cjs (UC1). 2) CONTAIN: Kill the detached node process, isolate the host, quarantine the NodePackages directory, and rotate all reachable credentials and wallet/crypto secrets (second stage is a wallet stealer/RAT). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the second-stage hash across the fleet, check the NvmProtocal/LaunchAgent/systemd persistence (UC3), and review network telemetry (UC2) for follow-on C2 beyond the two known IPs.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "NodePackages" and ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.

date: 2026/05/02

logsource:
    category: file_access

            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:

            - '\Exodus.exe'

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

CryptoBandits curl beacon over Tor SOCKS5 proxy to .onion C2 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the clipper's C2 channel: curl invoked with --socks5-hostname against the bundled Tor proxy on localhost:9050, talking to .onion endpoints /route.php, /recvf.php, /stub.php. This is the exact beacon/upload/payload-pull mechanism described for the CryptoBandits clipper. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim curl command shape (--socks5-hostname + localhost:9050) plus the named C2 endpoints /route.php, /recvf.php, /stub.php; curl talking SOCKS5 to a local Tor port is near-zero in normal enterprise use. Cross-checked against thehackernews.com and securityweek.com write-ups of the same campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html • https://www.securityweek.com/cryptobandits-malware-doubles-as-a-backdoor-abuses-tor/ • https://gbhackers.com/crypto-clipper-uses-windows-script/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or pentester using curl through a local Tor SOCKS proxy for testing
  • Privacy-tooling that wraps curl over Tor (e.g. torsocks demos)
  • Security researcher detonating samples in a monitored lab
  • Legitimate onion-service health-check scripts in a privacy-focused org
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("torsocks","\\dev\\","pentest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full curl command line and the parent process — confirm the .onion host and which endpoint (/route.php=beacon, /recvf.php=screenshot upload, /stub.php=payload pull). Check if parent is wscript.exe/cscript.exe running from C:\Users\Public\Documents. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill curl and any ugate.exe (renamed Tor) process, block outbound to 127.0.0.1:9050 listener process. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for ugate.exe, scheduled tasks referencing C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.xml, dropped .js payloads, and 'cfile' artifact; sweep the fleet for the worm SHA-256s.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--socks5-hostname" and ProcessCommandLine has "9050"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".onion", "/route.php", "/recvf.php", "/stub.php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--socks5-hostname" and CommandLine has "9050"
| where CommandLine has_any (".onion", "/route.php", "/recvf.php", "/stub.php")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
title: CryptoBandits curl Beacon over Tor SOCKS5 to .onion C2
id: 8f3a1c2d-4b5e-4f6a-9c7d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
status: experimental

Renamed Tor binary ugate.exe / Tor masquerade launched on endpoint AICommand & Control High
Detects the clipper's portable Tor client, deployed as a renamed binary 'ugate.exe' run in a hidden window to provide the local SOCKS5 proxy. Also catches future renames by matching the Tor original-filename metadata when the on-disk name is not tor.exe. Rationale: ugate.exe is the article's explicitly named renamed Tor binary; the metadata-masquerade clause (OriginalFileName=tor.exe but on-disk name differs) generalizes to defeat trivial renames while staying article-grounded. Corroborated by securityaffairs.com and securityweek.com naming ugate.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://securityaffairs.com/193860/uncategorized/tor-based-clipper-malware-targets-wallet-seed-phrases.html • https://www.securityweek.com/cryptobandits-malware-doubles-as-a-backdoor-abuses-tor/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately running the Tor Browser bundle (tor.exe under its real name — excluded)
  • An internal tool that legitimately bundles a renamed Tor client for privacy
  • Security testing of Tor-based tooling in a sanctioned lab
  • Threat-intel analyst detonating the sample
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary's SHA-256 against the worm hashes; check the parent (script host) and whether a SOCKS5 listener on 127.0.0.1:9050 appeared. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate ugate.exe, and capture the binary for analysis before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: look for the curl --socks5-hostname beacon, the scheduled-task XML in C:\Users\Public\Documents, dropped .js clipper files, and propagate the hash to a fleet-wide sweep.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
   or (ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "tor.exe" and FileName !~ "tor.exe")
   or (ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Tor" and FileName !~ "tor.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ugate.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine

Scheduled task created from JScript payload XML in Public\Documents staging folder AIInstallation High
Detects the worm's persistence: schtasks /create importing an XML task definition from C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.xml, matching the article's five-character folder/file naming convention used for both the worm and stealer tasks. Rationale: Built directly from the article's verbatim Defender hunting query (Block 1): schtasks /create /xml against the C:\Users\Public\Documents\[a-z]{4,6}\[a-z]{4,6}.xml path with the 5-character naming signature — legitimate software almost never stages task XML under Public\Documents with random 5-char names. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin script importing a task XML that happens to live under Public\Documents (rare)
  • Third-party installer staging a task XML in a public path
  • Backup/EDR agent registering tasks from a shared documents path
  • Lab detonation of the sample
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the task name (/tn) and the XML path; read the XML's Actions block to see which JScript file (C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.js) it launches and under wscript/cscript. 2) Contain: delete both worm and stealer scheduled tasks, isolate host, remove the staging folder. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks pointing into Public\Documents fleet-wide; correlate with ugate.exe and the curl Tor beacon; check for USB-insertion-triggered duplicate task that re-spreads to removable media.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "/xml"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "/xml"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, CommandLine

WScript/CScript executing dropped JScript clipper from Public\Documents staging folder AIInstallation High
Detects the clipper/stealer launch: wscript.exe or cscript.exe running one of the two obfuscated .js payloads dropped under C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\, matching the five-character folder and script naming convention. Rationale: Combines two article-specific facts — script-host (WScript/ActiveX) execution and the two .js payloads dropped under C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char> with a 5-character folder/script naming convention. The path+naming regex makes it specific to this campaign rather than generic script execution. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/crypto-clipper-uses-windows-script/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
ATT&CKT1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise automation storing .js under a public path (uncommon and usually named, not 5-random-char)
  • An admin troubleshooting script dropped temporarily in Public\Documents
  • Software installer leaving a JScript helper in a public folder
  • Sample detonation in a sandbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: copy the .js path and hash; confirm the parent (often the worm executable or explorer via .lnk) and whether ugate.exe/curl beacon followed within ~60s. 2) Contain: kill the wscript/cscript process tree, isolate the host, quarantine the .js and the staging folder. 3) Hunt: dump the deobfuscated script for the .onion C2 and EVAL handler; sweep for the scheduled-task XML, the worm SHA-256s, and any child cmd/powershell spawned by these script hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine

Microsoft Defender exclusion added for clipper staging folder or script-host binaries AIInstallation High
Detects the worm excluding its payloads from Defender scanning — registry writes to the Windows Defender Exclusions key covering C:\Users\Public\Documents or the binaries used by the stealer (wscript/cscript/ugate/curl). Maps to the article's ProcessExclusion/PathExclusion behaviors. Rationale: Article states the worm 'delivers file-based payloads and excludes them from Defender scanning' and lists Behavior:Win64/ProcessExclusion.STA / PathExclusion.STA; anchoring on the Defender Exclusions registry key plus the campaign's staging path and binaries makes this high-fidelity. Falcon left empty — FDR's AsepValueUpdate covers autostart, not arbitrary Defender-exclusion registry writes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/cryptobandits-malware-doubles-as-a-backdoor-abuses-tor/
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin or GPO legitimately excluding a Public\Documents share for a line-of-business app
  • EDR/AV migration tooling writing exclusion entries
  • Developer excluding a build output folder that happens to be under Public
  • Backup software adding exclusions for its staging area
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe", "msmpeng.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "mpcmdrun.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process that wrote the exclusion (legit GPO/SCCM vs. a script host or unsigned binary) and exactly what was excluded. 2) Contain: remove the malicious exclusion, isolate the host, re-scan the previously excluded path. 3) Hunt: examine the excluded folder for the dropped .js/ugate.exe/cfile artifacts; correlate with scheduled-task creation and the Tor curl beacon; sweep for the same exclusion pattern fleet-wide.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions"
| where RegistryValueName has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
   or RegistryValueName has_any ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "ugate.exe", "curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has "\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Exclusions"
| where RegistryValue has "\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\"
   or RegistryValue has_any ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "ugate.exe", "curl.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

    - attack.t1562.001
logsource:

detection:

            - '\Users\Public\Documents'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:*\\Windows*Defender\\Exclusions\\* (@TargetObject:*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\* OR @TargetObject:*\\users\\public\\documents\\* OR @TargetObject:*wscript.exe* OR @TargetObject:*cscript.exe* OR @TargetObject:*ugate.exe* OR @TargetObject:*curl.exe*)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Exclusions*" (Registry.registry_value_name="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_name="*wscript.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_name="*cscript.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_name="*ugate.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_name="*curl.exe*") by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

USB worm propagation: burst of .lnk shortcuts created by non-Explorer process AIDelivery Medium
Detects the worm's self-spreading step — scanning removable/document folders and creating a malicious .lnk per harvested .doc/.xlsx/.pdf while hiding the originals. Fires when a single non-Explorer process mass-creates .lnk files across several folders in a short window. Rationale: Article describes the worm scanning for .doc/.xlsx/.pdf, hiding originals, and creating same-named .lnk shortcuts that point to the worm payload; a non-Explorer process mass-creating .lnk across multiple folders is the observable signature. Threshold/temporal so no Sigma emitted. Cross-checked vs vpncentral and thenextweb USB-worm coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html • https://thenextweb.com/news/microsoft-crypto-clipper-usb-malware-tor-cryptocurrency-theft
ATT&CKT1091 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/sync tool regenerating shortcuts across folders
  • Software installer creating many Start Menu .lnk entries (usually under ProgramData)
  • User/script bulk-creating shortcuts on a share
  • Roaming-profile or folder-redirection tooling rebuilding shortcuts at logon
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the creating process and a sample .lnk target — worm .lnk point to an executable/script (often with hidden-window args) rather than the original document; confirm originals were set hidden. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the writing process, and warn against opening .lnk on the affected media/share. 3) Hunt: check removable-media insertion events and the USB-spreading scheduled task; sweep shares for same-named doc+.lnk pairs and for the worm SHA-256s.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe", "onedrive.exe", "msiexec.exe", "setup.exe", "svchost.exe")
| summarize LnkFolders = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFolders = make_set(FolderPath, 10), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where LnkFolders >= 5   // worm creates one .lnk per harvested document
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk"
| where ActingProcessName !has "explorer.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "OneDrive.exe"
| summarize LnkFolders = dcount(TargetFilePath), SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where LnkFolders >= 5
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.lnk OR *.LNK) -@Image:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.exe OR *\\OneDrive.exe OR *\\msiexec.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.lnk$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(explorer|onedrive|msiexec)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=lnkCount))
| lnkCount >= 5
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as lnk_paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as files from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("explorer.exe","onedrive.exe","msiexec.exe","setup.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where lnk_paths >= 5 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Tor EVAL backdoor: script-host clipper spawning command interpreters AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the backdoor capability — the JScript clipper (wscript/cscript running from C:\Users\Public\Documents) spawning cmd/powershell/curl/mshta in response to a C2 EVAL command. This is the financially-motivated stealer pivoting into remote code execution. Rationale: Article describes the checkC2Command/EVAL function executing attacker-supplied JScript at runtime ('lightweight backdoor'); detecting the script-host clipper (parent cmdline rooted in the Public\Documents staging folder) spawning interpreters captures that pivot. Falcon clause drops the parent-path constraint (FDR ProcessRollup2 lacks parent command line) — slightly broader, note for tuning. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/cryptobandits-malware-doubles-as-a-backdoor-abuses-tor/ • https://gbhackers.com/crypto-clipper-uses-windows-script/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise .js automation under a public path that legitimately calls cmd/powershell
  • Admin troubleshooting script in Public\Documents shelling out
  • Software setup helper using a script host to run a post-install command
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line — EVAL payloads typically run discovery (whoami, net, dir), download, or persistence commands; note the spawning .js path. 2) Contain: kill the full wscript/cscript→child tree, isolate the host, and snapshot for IR (the C2 may push further commands). 3) Hunt: pull the C2 'cfile' artifact and decode the script's EVAL handler; review all children of script hosts rooted in Public\Documents over the last 30 days; correlate with the Tor beacon timing.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "curl.exe", "mshta.exe", "cscript.exe", "wscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "curl.exe", "mshta.exe", "cscript.exe", "wscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

PowerShell screen capture spawned by clipper script host (collection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the clipper's screenshot collection — PowerShell using the CopyFromScreen/System.Drawing screen-capture APIs, launched by the wscript/cscript clipper or from the Public\Documents staging context. The malware grabs five screenshots ten seconds apart and uploads them over Tor. Rationale: Article lists 'screen-capture commands in PowerShell' as a strong defender signal and describes five timed screenshots uploaded over Tor; CopyFromScreen/System.Drawing is the canonical .NET screenshot API, and gating on the script-host parent (or Public\Documents staging context) keeps it specific to this campaign rather than generic PowerShell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thenextweb.com/news/microsoft-crypto-clipper-usb-malware-tor-cryptocurrency-theft
ATT&CKT1113
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT remote-support tooling that screenshots via PowerShell
  • Monitoring/screenshot-on-event automation launched from a script
  • RMM agent capturing screen for diagnostics
  • Sample detonation in a lab
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("screenconnect.exe", "teamviewer.exe", "rmm.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the screenshot cadence (5 captures ~10s apart) and the parent script host; check for the curl /recvf.php upload over Tor shortly after. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the script-host→PowerShell tree, and assume on-screen wallet/credential data was captured — force credential and wallet rotation. 3) Hunt: locate temp image files written before upload, the .onion C2 in the script, and correlate with clipboard/seed-phrase exfil; sweep for the worm hashes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "CopyFromScreen"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "System.Drawing" and ProcessCommandLine has "Bitmap" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Graphics", "Screen"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "CopyFromScreen"
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "System.Drawing" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "Bitmap")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe") or ParentProcessCommandLine has "\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or SHA1 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or MD5 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or SHA1 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or MD5 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8")

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable component exposure: org.hl7.fhir.utilities <= 6.9.9 / CVE-2026-55471
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-55471: HAPI FHIR: XXE in XsltUtilities.saxonTransform
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Blind XXE / SSRF: FHIR Java process fetches external DTD or XSLT stylesheet — CVE-2026-55471 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XXE parameter-entity OOB exfil: rare/long-label DNS callback from FHIR Java host — CVE-2026-55471
Blind XXE / SSRF: FHIR Java process fetches external DTD or XSLT stylesheet — CVE-2026-55471 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the exploitation side-effect of the unhardened Saxon TransformerFactory: with ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/STYLESHEET unset, the parser resolves external DTDs and stylesheets, so the FHIR/Java server makes an outbound request to an attacker URL ending in .dtd/.xsl/.xslt. Backend FHIR servers rarely fetch remote stylesheets, making this high-signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's root cause — saxonTransform resolving external DTD/stylesheet because ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/STYLESHEET are unset — expressed as a java-process / proxy egress to a .dtd/.xsl/.xslt URL, with public-DTD hosts (w3.org/oasis) filtered to cut benign XSLT toolchains. Falcon/Datadog fall back to java→public-IP since FDR/Sysmon network events carry no URL path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/ca.uhn.hapi.fhir/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/CVE-2026-55471/ • https://saxonica.plan.io/issues/4729
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java applications legitimately fetching remote XSLT stylesheets for report rendering
  • Document/IG publishing pipelines resolving public DTDs (already filtered for w3.org/oasis/docbook)
  • Internal CI servers running XSLT transforms against an internal artifact repo over HTTP
  • RemoteUrl unpopulated by Defender when web content filtering is off, causing under-detection rather than FP
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("w3.org","oasis-open.org","docbook.org","xml.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the destination host/URL and whether it is attacker-controlled (new domain, raw IP, recently registered); confirm the initiating process is the FHIR/Java service and correlate to a preceding inbound XML POST (UC 1). 2) Contain: block the destination at egress proxy/firewall and isolate the FHIR host if the fetched resource looks like an attacker DTD; capture the JVM's outbound connection list. 3) Hunt: check DeviceFileEvents on that host for java.exe reads of sensitive paths (file:// general-entity disclosure) and run the DNS-callback UC for parameter-entity OOB exfil.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")

XXE parameter-entity OOB exfil: rare/long-label DNS callback from FHIR Java host — CVE-2026-55471 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the out-of-band exfiltration channel of the blind XXE: a parameter-entity (<!ENTITY % p SYSTEM ...>) smuggles local file contents into a DNS subdomain label, producing a first-seen external domain or an abnormally long leftmost DNS label sourced from the FHIR/Java process. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit parameter-entity OOB primitive (<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://...">) by hunting the DNS side-channel from the java process: first-seen external domain (Defender) or 30+ char leftmost label (Sentinel/Falcon/Splunk DNS-exfil heuristic). Datadog left empty — Sysmon DNS (EID 22) is not in the shipped sysmon event set. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud/CDN telemetry domains that use long hashed leftmost labels (telemetry, antivirus reputation lookups)
  • Legitimate Java apps doing service discovery against long auto-generated hostnames
  • First-seen anti-join firing on a newly onboarded but benign integration endpoint
  • DNS over a corporate resolver that rewrites/long-encodes names
Suppression filter
| where not(DnsQuery has_any ("akamai","cloudfront","azureedge","trafficmanager","windowsupdate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode/inspect the long DNS label — base16/base32-looking content strongly indicates file exfil; confirm the source host runs the vulnerable FHIR/Java service and correlate to a recent inbound XML POST. 2) Contain: sinkhole the parent domain at the resolver, isolate the host if the label decodes to recognizable file content, and rotate secrets the service account could read. 3) Hunt: enumerate all distinct external domains the java process queried in the last 7 days, and check the network-egress UC for the matching attacker-DTD fetch that seeded the parameter entity.
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
    | where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RemoteUrl
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where isnotempty(DnsQuery)
| where DnsQuery !endswith "in-addr.arpa" and DnsQuery !endswith ".arpa"
| extend LeftLabel = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[0])
| where strlen(LeftLabel) >= 30   // 30+ char leftmost label = data smuggled into a DNS subdomain by XXE parameter-entity OOB
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, LeftLabelLen = strlen(LeftLabel)
| order by LeftLabelLen desc

Vulnerable component exposure: org.hl7.fhir.utilities <= 6.9.9 / CVE-2026-55471 AIExploitation High
Proactive exposure hunt for hosts running the affected HAPI FHIR utilities library (vulnerable <= 6.9.9, fixed in 6.9.10) that contains the unhardened saxonTransform XXE. Surfaces the attack surface so it can be patched before exploitation. Rationale: Uses the corroborated affected package (ca.uhn.hapi.fhir:org.hl7.fhir.utilities) and CVE id (CVE-2026-55471, vulnerable <= 6.9.9, fixed 6.9.10) directly against TVM/Vulnerabilities inventory. Empty for Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch — vulnerability inventory is not part of FDR event types or the listed Datadog/CloudWatch sources. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/ca.uhn.hapi.fhir/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/CVE-2026-55471/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM reporting a transitive jar that is actually shaded/relocated and not reachable via saxonTransform
  • Dev/test build hosts with the library present but no exposed FHIR endpoint
  • Inventory lag where a host already upgraded to 6.9.10 still shows the old version until next scan
  • A vendored copy embedded in a fat-jar that TVM version-detects imprecisely
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually exposes a FHIR service that routes untrusted XML through XsltUtilities.saxonTransform (IG-publisher, validator, conversion utilities are the documented consumers) versus the library merely being on disk. 2) Contain: prioritize internet-facing FHIR servers for upgrade to org.hl7.fhir.utilities 6.9.10; where patching lags, place a WAF rule blocking XML with DOCTYPE/ENTITY on FHIR endpoints (see UC 1). 3) Hunt: for each exposed vulnerable host, run the inbound-payload, SSRF-egress, and DNS-callback UCs over the last 30 days to check for prior exploitation.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crypto-clipper fake sniper-bot binary execution (silke / SniperBot / Sniper_TradingBot) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the Rust-based clipboard-hijacker payloads and their fake Solana/Pump.fun 'sniper bot' droppers from the Check Point 'fake reputation' campaign, matched by the campaign's specific file names and 14 known SHA256 hashes. Fires the moment any host runs one of the named binaries or a hash-matched sample. Rationale: Anchored on the campaign's exact payload names (silkebin.exe, silke.exe, SniperBot_Premium(Free).exe, Sniper_TradingBot.Premium(Trial).exe) and all 14 SHA256 hashes from Check Point's IOC appendix (Windows clipper, .NET loader, macOS clipper+loader) — file-name+hash matches are maximally high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/from-stars-to-upvotes-fake-reputation-fueling-a-crypto-clipboard-hijacker/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/crypto-clipboard-hijacker-fake/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/malware-campaign-uses-virustotal-manipulation-legitimate-news-sites-to-gain-reputation
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1115
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or threat-intel team detonating the sample in a managed sandbox/VM that ships EDR telemetry
  • IR responder copying a captured sample named silke.exe/silkebin.exe onto a forensic workstation
  • AV/EDR quarantine-and-restore actions that briefly re-materialize the named binary
  • An unrelated legitimate internal tool coincidentally named silke.exe (rare; hash will not match)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALLAB","IR-") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm FileName/SHA256 against the IOC list, pull FolderPath and the full process tree (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a Downloads/Temp origin and a sniper-bot parent confirms the lure. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and treat any crypto wallet recently used on it as compromised — clipboard substitution means outbound transactions may already be redirected; advise the user to verify destination addresses out-of-band. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC for %APPDATA%\silke\silke.exe persistence and Startup-folder shortcut, and sweep the org for the other 13 hashes and the GitHub-origin downloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("silkebin.exe","silke.exe","SniperBot_Premium(Free).exe","Sniper_TradingBot.Premium(Trial).exe"))

Crypto-clipper Windows persistence: silke.exe drop to %APPDATA%\silke + Startup shortcut AIInstallation High
Detects the clipper installing itself for persistence by copying its executable to %APPDATA%\silke\silke.exe and creating a logon shortcut in the Startup folder, as documented by Check Point. This is the install-time foothold that survives reboot and re-arms clipboard monitoring. Rationale: Uses Check Point's exact persistence path %APPDATA%\silke\silke.exe plus the Startup-folder shortcut written by the silke/silkebin parent — a hard-coded, non-generic path makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/from-stars-to-upvotes-fake-reputation-fueling-a-crypto-clipboard-hijacker/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/crypto-clipboard-hijacker-fake/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1115
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst restoring a sample into a roaming-profile path during reverse engineering
  • Roaming-profile sync (FSLogix/UE-V) re-creating the file across session hosts after an initial infection (still a true positive, just duplicated)
  • Legitimate vendor app coincidentally using an 'silke' AppData folder (no known vendor uses this name)
  • Backup/EDR remediation tooling re-staging the quarantined file
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the %APPDATA%\silke\silke.exe write and identify InitiatingProcessFileName (should be silkebin.exe or the sniper-bot dropper); enumerate the Startup-folder .lnk target. 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the silke folder and Startup shortcut, kill running silke processes, and reset/migrate any crypto wallets used on the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 execution hits, check for the macOS LaunchAgent variant on Mac fleet, and sweep for the GitHub/SourceForge download origin (UC3).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where (FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\silke\" and FileName =~ "silke.exe")
    or (FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" and FileName endswith ".lnk" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("silkebin.exe","silke.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Roaming\silke\" and TargetFileName =~ "silke.exe")
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" and TargetFileName endswith ".lnk" and ActingProcessName has_any ("silkebin.exe","silke.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crypto-clipper delivery: fake sniper-bot installer downloaded from threat-actor GitHub/SourceForge AIDelivery Medium
Detects the delivery stage where users download the campaign's fake Solana/Pump.fun sniper-bot installers from the threat actor's GitHub accounts or SourceForge projects, keyed on the specific installer file names and the actor's six GitHub account handles appearing in the download origin URL. Rationale: Pivots on the actor's six named GitHub handles (Decryptor-j, crash-predictor1, roblox-script1, hack-scripts, stake-mines) in the download-origin URL plus the exact installer file names from Check Point — catches the lure at delivery, before execution. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/from-stars-to-upvotes-fake-reputation-fueling-a-crypto-clipboard-hijacker/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/malware-campaign-uses-virustotal-manipulation-legitimate-news-sites-to-gain-reputation

  • Roblox/gaming users downloading benign script tools with similarly themed repo names
  • Web-proxy logging the URL but the download being blocked by SmartScreen (still worth triage)

Crypto-clipper macOS persistence: com.example LaunchAgent + ~/launch.sh watchdog AIInstallation High
Detects the macOS variant of the clipper establishing persistence via a LaunchAgent plist (com.example..plist with RunAtLoad/KeepAlive) and a ~/launch.sh watchdog wrapper, as detailed by Check Point. Targets Mac endpoints reporting to Defender XDR / Falcon. Rationale: Uses Check Point's exact macOS persistence artifacts: LaunchAgent plist prefixed com.example with RunAtLoad/KeepAlive and the ~/launch.sh watchdog wrapper — the plist path is distinctive enough to alert on. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/from-stars-to-upvotes-fake-reputation-fueling-a-crypto-clipboard-hijacker/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/crypto-clipboard-hijacker-fake/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1115
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers shipping/testing sample LaunchAgents using Apple's placeholder bundle id 'com.example.*' (genuinely common in tutorials and template projects)
  • Generic launch.sh scripts in user home/dev project directories unrelated to malware
  • CI/automation tooling that writes user LaunchAgents named com.example during testing
  • MDM/management agents staging LaunchAgents (different reverse-DNS prefix, so usually excluded)
Suppression filter
DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Xcode","node","npm","python3")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the com.example plist, confirm RunAtLoad/KeepAlive and that ProgramArguments point at a non-standard binary or ~/launch.sh; correlate to the macOS clipper hash b71efdebd0ca3563e67edb7ad59358a6b8f013b219ad65033efcf48fd1c86619. 2) Contain: isolate the Mac, unload and delete the LaunchAgent (launchctl bootout) and ~/launch.sh, kill the watchdog loop, and rotate any crypto wallets used on the host. 3) Hunt: sweep the Mac fleet for the same plist/launch.sh, check Windows fleet for the silke persistence variant (UC2), and review the download source (UC3).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and FileName startswith "com.example" and FileName endswith ".plist")
    or (FileName =~ "launch.sh" and FolderPath !has "/usr/" and FolderPath !has "/opt/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and TargetFileName startswith "com.example" and TargetFileName endswith ".plist")
    or (TargetFileName =~ "launch.sh" and TargetFilePath !has "/usr/" and TargetFilePath !has "/opt/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
