Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Critical

Junior Hacker Used Tailscale and OpenSSH to Keep Access After His C2 Went Offline

The Hacker News
2026-06-17 19 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A French-speaking attacker broke into a small French automotive business, planted a keylogger, and stole banking and email credentials. Ordinary stuff, until one move near the end. Before his command-and-control server went dark, he installed OpenSSH and Tailscale on a victim's machine, building a way back in that did not run through the C2 at all. When the Havoc server went offline the next

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] wscript.exe executing .vbs from user staging folder (Poisson VBScript stager)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Junior Hacker Used Tailscale and OpenSSH to Keep Access After His C2 Went Offlin
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Tailscale mesh-VPN client install/exec on Windows endpoint (Operation Poisson parallel persistence) · [LLM] OpenSSH Server feature install / sshd service creation on Windows workstation · [LLM] SSH authorized_keys provisioning / ssh-keygen on Windows endpoint (key-based backdoor) · [LLM] Scheduled task at logon with highest privileges launching a script interpreter · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Tailscale WireGuard egress (UDP 41641 / CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 / *.ts.net) out-of-band C2 channel · [LLM] OpenSSH reverse tunnel (ssh -R) to external host — out-of-band C2 fallback · [LLM] DuckDNS dynamic-DNS resolution from endpoint (Havoc/Poisson C2 infrastructure) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] powercfg standby/monitor-timeout set to never (keep host awake for keylogger harvesting) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change
Tailscale mesh-VPN client install/exec on Windows endpoint (Operation Poisson parallel persistence) AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Tailscale binary running or being installed on a workstation, the exact post-compromise persistence move Poisson used to keep access independent of his Havoc C2. Tailscale is rare on managed endpoints and its presence on a non-IT asset is a high-value out-of-band-access signal. Rationale: Article and Cato/SOC Prime writeups state Poisson installed Tailscale to join the victim host to his private tailnet; tailscale.exe/tailscaled.exe and 'tailscale up'/--authkey are the literal install/join strings. Corroborated by Tailscale docs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/operation-poisson-breaking-down-an-entire-cybercriminal-operation/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/attacker-establishes-persistent-access-to-french-business-using-openssh-and-tailscale
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/devops staff using Tailscale for legitimate remote admin on engineering boxes
  • MSP/contractor onboarding a sanctioned mesh-VPN
  • Developer self-installing Tailscale for home-lab access
  • Sanctioned Tailscale rollout on a pilot device group
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["IT-ADMIN-01","DEVOPS-BUILD-01"]))   // exclude assets with an approved Tailscale entitlement (replace with your sanctioned-host watchlist)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the asset has no approved Tailscale/mesh-VPN entitlement; pull AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine and any --authkey value, and check whether install coincided with a malware/Havoc detection on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the device, run 'tailscale logout' / uninstall, revoke the tailnet auth key with the Tailscale admin (if org tenant) and block *.tailscale.com/*.ts.net egress for the asset group. 3) Hunt: pivot to OpenSSH install, sshd service, authorized_keys writes, scheduled-task logon persistence and powercfg changes on the same host and timeframe — Poisson layered all of these together.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("tailscale.exe","tailscaled.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tailscale up","login.tailscale.com","--authkey","tailscale.exe up")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\tailscale.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\tailscaled.exe"
     or CommandLine has_any ("tailscale up","login.tailscale.com","--authkey"))
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Tailscale Mesh-VPN Client Execution on Windows Endpoint
id: a1f4c2e0-1b2c-4d3e-9f10-111111111111
description: Detects execution or install of the Tailscale client (tailscale.exe/tailscaled.exe) used by Operation Poisson for out-of-band parallel persistence.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/junior-hacker-used-tailscale-and.html
  - https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\tailscale.exe'
      - '\tailscaled.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'tailscale up'
      - 'login.tailscale.com'
      - '--authkey'
  condition: selection_img or selection_cmd
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\tailscale.exe OR *\\Tailscale.exe OR *\\tailscaled.exe OR *\\Tailscaled.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*tailscale\ up* OR *login.tailscale.com* OR *--authkey*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/\\tailscaled?\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/tailscale\s+up|login\.tailscale\.com|--authkey/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("tailscale.exe","tailscaled.exe") OR Processes.process="*tailscale up*" OR Processes.process="*login.tailscale.com*" OR Processes.process="*--authkey*") AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$","SYSTEM","LOCAL SERVICE","NETWORK SERVICE") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("tailscale.exe","tailscaled.exe") OR Processes.process="*tailscale up*" OR Processes.process="*login.tailscale.com*" OR Processes.process="*--authkey*") AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$","SYSTEM","LOCAL SERVICE","NETWORK SERVICE") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Tailscale WireGuard egress (UDP 41641 / CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 / *.ts.net) out-of-band C2 channel AICommand & Control Medium
Network-side companion to the Tailscale process detection: surfaces the encrypted mesh tunnel itself — outbound UDP 41641, coordination/DERP traffic to login.tailscale.com / *.ts.net, and peer IPs in the 100.64.0.0/10 CGNAT range Poisson used to reach the host with no exposed ports and no C2. Rationale: Article describes reaching the host 'over Tailscale's encrypted mesh with no C2 and no exposed ports'; UDP 41641, login.tailscale.com and the 100.64.0.0/10 tailnet range (pre-extracted IOC 100.100.100.2 sits in this range) are the confirmed Tailscale network fingerprints per Tailscale docs. Cross-checked against: • https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/faq/firewall-ports • https://tailscale.com/docs/concepts/tailscale-ip-addresses • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Tailscale users on IT/dev assets generating legitimate 41641 traffic
  • Carrier-grade NAT on the corporate WAN legitimately using 100.64.0.0/10 internally
  • Approved site-to-site mesh-VPN pilots
  • Personal devices on BYOD segments running Tailscale
Suppression filter
| where ipv4_is_in_any_range(SourceIP, "100.64.0.0/10") == false   // drop internal CGNAT-to-CGNAT chatter if your WAN legitimately uses 100.64/10
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName for the 41641 flow — if not tailscaled.exe on an approved host, treat as malicious; map peer IPs in 100.64.0.0/10 to identify the attacker relay. 2) Contain: block UDP 41641 and *.tailscale.com/*.ts.net egress for the affected segment, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate the tunnel window against gaps in Havoc/DuckDNS C2 beaconing — Poisson's Tailscale path stayed up the 18 days his C2 was offline; look for SSH activity riding inside the same window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemotePort == 41641 and Protocol =~ "Udp")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("login.tailscale.com","controlplane.tailscale.com",".ts.net")
   or ipv4_is_in_any_range(RemoteIP, "100.64.0.0/10")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DestinationPort == 41641)
   or DestinationHostName has_any ("login.tailscale.com","controlplane.tailscale.com",".ts.net")
   or ipv4_is_in_any_range(DestinationIP, "100.64.0.0/10")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DestinationHostName, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenSSH Server feature install / sshd service creation on Windows workstation AIInstallation High
Detects OpenSSH Server being added to a Windows workstation (Add-WindowsCapability OpenSSH.Server, sshd service creation, sshd.exe running) — the second leg of Poisson's parallel persistence. OpenSSH Server on a non-server endpoint is, per Cato's own hunting list, rarely legitimate. Rationale: Article and Cato hunting list explicitly: 'Alert when OpenSSH Server installs on a Windows workstation, which is rarely legitimate.' Add-WindowsCapability OpenSSH.Server and sshd service creation are the concrete install paths. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/attacker-establishes-persistent-access-to-french-business-using-openssh-and-tailscale
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin enabling OpenSSH for legitimate remote management
  • Devops/Ansible workflows that provision OpenSSH on Windows hosts
  • Golden-image build pipeline that bakes in OpenSSH.Server
  • Developer using VS Code Remote-SSH server component
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible.exe","ssm-agent.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "SRV-"   // exclude managed servers / config-mgmt provisioners
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm OpenSSH Server is not an approved management tool on this asset class; check the parent process and account that ran Add-WindowsCapability/sc create sshd, and whether it occurred outside change windows. 2) Contain: stop and disable the sshd service, isolate the host, and review C:\ProgramData\ssh\sshd_config plus firewall rules opened for port 22. 3) Hunt: immediately check authorized_keys files, ssh.exe -R reverse tunnels and Tailscale presence on the same host — Poisson chained OpenSSH + Tailscale in the same overnight session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("OpenSSH.Server","Add-WindowsCapability","Start-Service sshd","Set-Service sshd","sc create sshd","sc.exe create sshd")
   or FileName =~ "sshd.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has_any ("OpenSSH.Server","Add-WindowsCapability","Start-Service sshd","Set-Service sshd","sc create sshd")
     or NewProcessName endswith "\\sshd.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SSH authorized_keys provisioning / ssh-keygen on Windows endpoint (key-based backdoor) AIInstallation High
Detects creation or modification of SSH authorized_keys files (per-user .ssh\authorized_keys and ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys) and ssh-keygen execution — Poisson set up key-based SSH so he could log back in without a password after his C2 died. Rationale: Article: 'set up key-based SSH'. authorized_keys / administrators_authorized_keys (Windows OpenSSH admin key path) writes are the high-fidelity artifact of an SSH key backdoor; reviewer feedback #2 specifically flagged this gap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/
ATT&CKT1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin legitimately provisioning SSH key auth for remote management
  • Git/devops tooling writing per-user .ssh keys
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/DSC) deploying authorized_keys to managed hosts
  • Developer running ssh-keygen for a new project
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible.exe","dsc.exe","git.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-ansible","svc-deploy")   // exclude sanctioned config-mgmt key deployment
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the new authorized_keys content — capture the public key fingerprint/comment and the writing process/account; an attacker key has no matching corporate key inventory. 2) Contain: remove the unauthorized key entry, disable/stop sshd, isolate the host, and rotate the affected local account. 3) Hunt: search other hosts for the same public-key fingerprint, and correlate with OpenSSH install, ssh -R tunnels and Tailscale on the same asset/timeframe.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ ("authorized_keys","administrators_authorized_keys")
   or (FolderPath has ".ssh" and FileName !endswith ".tmp")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("authorized_keys","administrators_authorized_keys")
   or TargetFilePath has ".ssh"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenSSH reverse tunnel (ssh -R) to external host — out-of-band C2 fallback AICommand & Control High
Detects ssh.exe launched with a reverse-port-forward (-R) flag, the exact mechanism Poisson used to build a reverse tunnel that reached the victim machine with no exposed inbound ports. Reverse tunnels from an endpoint to an outside host are almost never legitimate. Rationale: Article and Cato hunting list: 'Look for ssh -R reverse tunnels heading to outside hosts.' The -R flag on ssh.exe is the literal, high-fidelity reverse-tunnel indicator; reviewer feedback #4 reinforces it. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/attacker-establishes-persistent-access-to-french-business-using-openssh-and-tailscale
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using ssh -R for a legitimate remote-debug/port-share to a known jump host
  • IT staff tunneling a service to an internal bastion
  • CI agent setting up a reverse tunnel to a build relay
  • Vendor support session using SSH reverse forwarding
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bastion.corp","jump.corp","127.0.0.1","localhost"))   // exclude sanctioned internal jump-host tunnels
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the -R argument and destination host/port from the command line; resolve the external host and check reputation — an unknown VPS (Poisson used a Berlin IONOS box) is a strong indicator. 2) Contain: kill the ssh.exe process, block egress to the destination IP, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate other outbound SSH from the estate to the same destination, and check the host for OpenSSH server install, authorized_keys backdoor and Tailscale — the reverse tunnel was one of several redundant doors.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "ssh.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-R\s+\S"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-R\s+\S"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

wscript.exe executing .vbs from user staging folder (Poisson VBScript stager) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for wscript/cscript running a .vbs file out of a user staging directory (AppData/Temp/Public/Downloads), the entry point of Poisson's in-memory chain (VBScript stager → PowerShell loader → .NET loader → Havoc Demon). The sandbox-evasion delay means the stager runs interactively from a staging path, not a signed install location. Rationale: Article: 'A VBScript stager with a sandbox-evasion delay decrypted a PowerShell loader'; Cato hunting list: 'Check for wscript.exe running .vbs files out of user staging folders.' Path + interpreter is the literal stager signature, distinct from generic Office-spawns-script rules. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/operation-poisson-breaking-down-an-entire-cybercriminal-operation/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that ship VBScript installers/updaters in Temp
  • Software deployment tools staging .vbs helpers in AppData
  • Login scripts copied to user profile folders
  • Admin troubleshooting scripts run from Downloads
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe")   // exclude known software-deployment VBScript helpers
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the .vbs file, decode it, and look for the staged PowerShell/.NET loader and decryption logic; check the parent (browser/archive/email) that dropped it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript chain, capture memory (Havoc Demon ran in-memory, no disk implant). 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for in-memory PowerShell loaders, Explorer.exe injection, scheduled-task logon persistence and the OpenSSH/Tailscale backdoor — all later stages of the same chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".vbs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppData","\\Temp\\","\\Public\\","Downloads","%TEMP%","%APPDATA%")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".vbs"
| where CommandLine has_any ("AppData","\\Temp\\","\\Public\\","Downloads","%TEMP%","%APPDATA%")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task at logon with highest privileges launching a script interpreter AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a scheduled task that triggers at logon with RunLevel Highest and launches a script interpreter (wscript/cscript/powershell/mshta/.vbs/.ps1) — Poisson's documented persistence: 'a scheduled task running at every logon with highest privileges.' Rationale: Article: 'a scheduled task running at every logon with highest privileges' and Cato hunting list: 'Flag scheduled tasks set to the highest privileges that launch script interpreters.' The /RL HIGHEST + /SC ONLOGON + interpreter triad is the literal persistence fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint-management agents creating at-logon highest-privilege maintenance tasks
  • Legitimate software updaters registering logon tasks via PowerShell
  • Admin login automation scripts
  • GPO/Intune-deployed scheduled tasks running a sanctioned .ps1
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("intunemanagementextension.exe","ccmexec.exe","gpscript.exe")   // exclude MDM/SCCM/GPO task provisioning
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task definition (action, trigger, principal); inspect the script it launches and where it lives (staging folder = malicious). 2) Contain: delete the task, isolate the host, and remove the referenced script/payload. 3) Hunt: the task likely re-launches the in-memory loader — check for Explorer.exe injection, OpenSSH/Tailscale persistence and the keylogger file on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create" and ProcessCommandLine has "highest" and ProcessCommandLine has "onlogon")
     or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask" and ProcessCommandLine has "Highest")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript","powershell","mshta",".vbs",".ps1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "create" and CommandLine has "highest" and CommandLine has "onlogon")
     or ((NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask" and CommandLine has "Highest")
| where CommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript","powershell","mshta",".vbs",".ps1")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task At-Logon Highest-Privilege Launching Script Interpreter
id: a7f4c2e0-7b2c-4d3e-9f10-777777777777
description: Detects schtasks/Register-ScheduledTask creating an at-logon highest-privilege task that runs a script interpreter, the Operation Poisson persistence move.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/junior-hacker-used-tailscale-and.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:

  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_schtasks:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'create'
      - 'highest'
      - 'onlogon'
  selection_payload:

      - 'wscript'
      - 'cscript'
      - 'powershell'
      - 'mshta'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.ps1'
  condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*create*) @CommandLine:(*highest* OR *HIGHEST*) @CommandLine:(*onlogon* OR *ONLOGON*) @CommandLine:(*wscript* OR *cscript* OR *powershell* OR *mshta* OR *.vbs* OR *.ps1*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/create/i CommandLine=/highest/i CommandLine=/onlogon/i CommandLine=/wscript|cscript|powershell|mshta|\.vbs|\.ps1/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*create*" AND Processes.process="*highest*" AND Processes.process="*onlogon*") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Register-ScheduledTask*" AND Processes.process="*Highest*")) AND (Processes.process IN ("*wscript*","*cscript*","*powershell*","*mshta*","*.vbs*","*.ps1*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*create*" AND Processes.process="*highest*" AND Processes.process="*onlogon*") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Register-ScheduledTask*" AND Processes.process="*Highest*")) AND (Processes.process IN ("*wscript*","*cscript*","*powershell*","*mshta*","*.vbs*","*.ps1*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
powercfg standby/monitor-timeout set to never (keep host awake for keylogger harvesting) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects powercfg disabling sleep/standby/monitor timeouts (set to 0 = never), the trick Poisson used so the machine never slept and his local keylogger kept harvesting. A distinctive, low-noise behaviour rarely seen outside of attacker tradecraft on user endpoints. Rationale: Article: 'ran powercfg to keep the machines from sleeping, so harvesting never paused' and Cato list: 'Watch for powercfg standby-timeout changes that keep machines awake.' Setting timeout to 0 is the literal, rarely-legitimate command. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/operation-poisson-breaking-down-an-entire-cybercriminal-operation/
ATT&CKT1653
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT setting kiosk/conference-room or always-on machines to never sleep
  • Power-plan management via GPO/Intune scripts
  • Long-running batch/render workstations configured to stay awake
  • Admin troubleshooting a sleep/wake issue
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe","ccmexec.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "KIOSK-"   // exclude policy-driven and kiosk always-on hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent process/account and whether the host is a sanctioned always-on asset; an interactive user account flipping standby to 0 on a normal workstation is suspicious. 2) Contain: revert the power policy, isolate the host if other indicators present. 3) Hunt: a local keylogger file is the likely reason — search the host for a small keystroke-log file in user folders and pivot to the wscript stager, scheduled task and OpenSSH/Tailscale persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "powercfg.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(standby|monitor|hibernate)-timeout-(ac|dc)\s+0\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powercfg.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(standby|monitor|hibernate)-timeout-(ac|dc)\s+0\b"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: powercfg Disabling Sleep/Standby Timeout (Keep Host Awake)
id: a8f4c2e0-8b2c-4d3e-9f10-888888888888
description: Detects powercfg setting standby/monitor/hibernate timeout to 0, used in Operation Poisson to keep the host awake for keylogger harvesting.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/junior-hacker-used-tailscale-and.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1653
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\powercfg.exe'
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)(standby|monitor|hibernate)-timeout-(ac|dc)\s+0\b'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\powercfg.exe OR *\\PowerCfg.exe OR *\\POWERCFG.EXE) @CommandLine:(*standby-timeout-ac\ 0* OR *standby-timeout-dc\ 0* OR *monitor-timeout-ac\ 0* OR *monitor-timeout-dc\ 0*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\powercfg\.exe$/i CommandLine=/(standby|monitor|hibernate)-timeout-(ac|dc)\s+0\b/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="powercfg.exe" AND (Processes.process="*standby-timeout-ac 0*" OR Processes.process="*standby-timeout-dc 0*" OR Processes.process="*monitor-timeout-ac 0*" OR Processes.process="*monitor-timeout-dc 0*" OR Processes.process="*hibernate-timeout-ac 0*") AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="powercfg.exe" AND (Processes.process="*standby-timeout-ac 0*" OR Processes.process="*standby-timeout-dc 0*" OR Processes.process="*monitor-timeout-ac 0*" OR Processes.process="*monitor-timeout-dc 0*" OR Processes.process="*hibernate-timeout-ac 0*") AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
DuckDNS dynamic-DNS resolution from endpoint (Havoc/Poisson C2 infrastructure) AICommand & Control Medium
Surfaces endpoint resolution of *.duckdns.org, the free dynamic-DNS provider Poisson used to front his Havoc C2. Cato's hunting list says to block DuckDNS outright; resolution from a corporate endpoint is a strong C2 indicator. Rationale: Article and pre-extracted IOC list name duckdns.org as the C2 fronting infra; Cato's hunting list explicitly says 'Block DuckDNS.' Endpoint resolution of *.duckdns.org is the concrete network IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-operation-poisson-analyzing-a-cybercriminals-entire-operation/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/operation-poisson-breaking-down-an-entire-cybercriminal-operation/
ATT&CKT1568 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/hobbyists with legitimate DuckDNS home-lab subdomains
  • IoT or self-hosted services using DuckDNS for remote access
  • Security researchers visiting a DuckDNS-hosted resource
  • Personal devices on guest/BYOD networks
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")   // browser lookups are likely user-driven; non-browser resolvers are the signal
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that initiated the DuckDNS lookup and the specific subdomain/resolved IP; non-browser processes resolving duckdns.org are high-confidence C2. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block *.duckdns.org at the resolver and block the resolved IP, isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: correlate the resolving host with Havoc Demon in-memory activity, then assume a quiet persistence layer (Tailscale/OpenSSH) exists and hunt it — the article's core lesson is the C2 is never the only door.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "duckdns.org"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "duckdns.org"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, IPAddresses=Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

Malicious JetBrains Plugins Steal AI API Keys as Chrome Extensions Capture Chatbot Chats

The Hacker News
2026-06-17 8 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a "coordinated malware campaign" on the JetBrains Marketplace that has published no less than 15 malicious plugins capable of exfiltrating artificial intelligence (AI) provider keys. "Every plugin poses as an AI coding assistant built on DeepSeek and other large language models, offering chat, commit messages, code review, bug finding, and unit tests,"

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002 T1555.003
IPs39.107.60.51

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious DeepSeek/CodeGPT JetBrains plugin written to IDE plugins directory · [LLM] PromptSnatcher malicious Chrome ad-blocker extension installed by ID
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] JetBrains IDE exfiltrating AI API keys to Aikido C2 39.107.60.51 · [LLM] PromptSnatcher Chrome extension exfiltrating AI chats to c.smartadblocker.com / c.abforbrowser.com · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
JetBrains IDE exfiltrating AI API keys to Aikido C2 39.107.60.51 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts JetBrains IDE processes (idea64.exe, pycharm64.exe, etc.) making outbound connections to the hardcoded plaintext-HTTP server 39.107.60.51 used by the 15 malicious DeepSeek/CodeGPT marketplace plugins to siphon the user-entered OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API key. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact attacker IP rather than generic IDE egress. Rationale: Pivots on the exact attacker IP 39.107.60.51 cross-confirmed by BleepingComputer and Aikido (plaintext-HTTP key exfil), making any connection to it inherently high-fidelity regardless of which of the 15 plugins is installed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/multiple-jetbrains-ide-plugins-caught-stealing-ai-keys • https://hackread.com/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-deepseek-openai-api-keys/
ATT&CKT1041 T1552
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or detonation host deliberately running a sample plugin
  • Threat-intel/IOC validation scanner reaching out to confirm the IP
  • Security researcher reproducing the campaign in a lab
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if the address is later reassigned to a benign service
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and InitiatingProcessFileName — confirm it is a JetBrains IDE (idea64.exe, pycharm64.exe, webstorm64.exe, etc.) and pull the user account; assume the AI provider API key entered in that IDE is compromised. 2) Contain: block 39.107.60.51 at the perimeter, isolate the host if non-sandbox, and immediately revoke/rotate the affected OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API keys. 3) Hunt: enumerate installed JetBrains plugins on the host and across the fleet for the 15 known package IDs; check billing/usage dashboards of the AI provider for anomalous spend indicating the stolen key is already being resold (LLMjacking).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious DeepSeek/CodeGPT JetBrains plugin written to IDE plugins directory AIDelivery Medium
Hunts file writes into the JetBrains plugins directory matching the display names of the 15 malicious marketplace plugins (DeepSeek/CodeGPT/AI Coder family). Surfaces installation of the supply-chain plugins before the API key is entered and exfiltrated. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious plugin display names from the article's 15-plugin list scoped to the JetBrains \plugins\ install path; deliberately hunting-tier because 'DeepSeek'/'CodeGPT' tokens can also match unrelated legitimate plugins, so analyst confirmation against the package IDs is required. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/multiple-jetbrains-ide-plugins-caught-stealing-ai-keys • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/
ATT&CKT1176.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing a legitimate DeepSeek or CodeGPT integration plugin (real 'CodeGPT' plugin exists)
  • JetBrains IDE auto-update rewriting an existing benign plugin folder with 'AI'/'Coder' in its name
  • Corporate-curated plugin repository pushing an approved AI assistant
  • Backup/sync tooling copying the plugins directory between machines
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("jetbrains.codeGPT","ee.carlrobert.codegpt"))   // exclude the legitimate CarlRobert CodeGPT plugin id
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the matched plugin folder and read META-INF/plugin.xml — compare the plugin id against the 15 known malicious package IDs (e.g. org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.my.code.tools, ord.cp.code.ai.kit); a match is a confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: uninstall the plugin, disconnect the host if any key was already entered, and rotate the developer's AI provider API keys. 3) Hunt: pivot the same host to UC 'JetBrains IDE exfiltrating AI API keys to 39.107.60.51' to confirm whether exfiltration already occurred, and sweep all developer endpoints for the same package IDs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\JetBrains\" and FolderPath has @"\plugins\"
| where FolderPath has_any ("DeepSeek","CodeGPT","AI Coder","AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","Coding Simple Tool")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("DeepSeek","CodeGPT","AI Coder","AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","Coding Simple Tool")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PromptSnatcher malicious Chrome ad-blocker extension installed by ID AIDelivery High
Hunts file writes into the Chrome Extensions directory for the two PromptSnatcher extension IDs (Smart Adblocker / Adblock for Browser) that intercept AI chatbot conversations. Pivots on the exact Web Store extension IDs, so any hit is the specific malicious add-on, not a generic extension install. Rationale: Chrome unpacks extensions to ...\User Data\<profile>\Extensions\<extension_id>\, so matching the two exact PromptSnatcher Web Store IDs (lowercase, case-stable) yields a clean alerting-grade signal with effectively no collisions. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/promptsnatcher-ad-blocker-extensions-steal-ai-chats/ • https://gbhackers.com/promptsnatcher-browser-extensions-abuse-ai/
ATT&CKT1176.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately (but unknowingly) installing the still-live Web Store extension for genuine ad-blocking — this is a true positive, not a benign FP, and should be treated as exposure
  • Enterprise GPO/force-install list deploying the extension org-wide before it was flagged
  • Roaming-profile sync replicating the extension folder to additional hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the extension ID and the Chrome profile/user; treat any AI chatbot session (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, etc.) on that profile as having been captured. 2) Contain: force-remove the extension via ExtensionInstallBlocklist GPO, add the two IDs to the browser blocklist fleet-wide, and have the user reset credentials/sessions for sensitive AI platforms. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'PromptSnatcher Chrome extension exfiltrating AI chats' to confirm egress to c.smartadblocker.com / c.abforbrowser.com, and inventory all endpoints for these two extension IDs.

| where FolderPath has_any ("iojpcjjdfhlcbgjnpngcmaojmlokmeii","jcbjcocinigpbgfpnhlpagidbmlngnnn")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("iojpcjjdfhlcbgjnpngcmaojmlokmeii","jcbjcocinigpbgfpnhlpagidbmlngnnn")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PromptSnatcher Chrome extension exfiltrating AI chats to c.smartadblocker.com / c.abforbrowser.com AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts DNS/network egress to the two PromptSnatcher operator C2 domains used to upload captured AI chatbot conversations and account-tier metadata. The C2 domains came from corroborating vendor write-ups (the article only said 'operator-controlled infrastructure'), making this the exfil-phase counterpart to the extension-install detection. Rationale: Uses the two C2 domains (c.smartadblocker.com / c.abforbrowser.com) surfaced by BleepingComputer/CyberSecurityNews corroboration of the article; matching on the registrable domain catches the exfil channel regardless of subdomain rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/promptsnatcher-ad-blocker-extensions-steal-ai-chats/ • https://gbhackers.com/promptsnatcher-browser-extensions-abuse-ai/ • https://cyberpress.org/ad-blockers-steal-ai-chats/
ATT&CKT1176.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the extension in a controlled lab
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or passive-DNS scanner resolving the domain for enrichment
  • Web proxy/DNS-filtering appliance pre-resolving the domain to render a block page
  • Domain later reclaimed/sinkholed by a vendor, causing benign resolutions
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the Chrome profile/user resolving the C2 domain; assume every AI chatbot conversation on that profile was uploaded (prompts up to 10k chars, responses up to 30k chars per the reporting). 2) Contain: sink/deny smartadblocker.com and abforbrowser.com at DNS/proxy, remove the offending extension (IDs iojpcjjdfhlcbgjnpngcmaojmlokmeii / jcbjcocinigpbgfpnhlpagidbmlngnnn), and reset sessions for sensitive AI platforms. 3) Hunt: correlate with the extension-install UC to find every host with these IDs, and review what was discussed in AI chats from affected users for data-exposure scoping.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("smartadblocker.com","abforbrowser.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("smartadblocker.com","abforbrowser.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

But when a vulnerability does drop — like MongoBleed earlier this year, which let attackers pull credentials and session tokens from server memory without authentication — anything internet-facing is immediately at risk. RDP password-guessing burst followed by successful logon on internet-facing host AIExploitation High
Hunts the RDP credential-guessing initial-access pattern the article calls out (RDP #5, BlueKeep, ransomware operators getting in via exposed RDP): a high volume of failed RemoteInteractive logons from a public IP, followed by a successful logon from that same IP to the same host within the attack window. Article-specific because it targets the exposed-RDP-to-compromise path, not generic auth failures. Rationale: Grounds on the article's explicit claim that 'credential guessing against exposed RDP remains one of the most reliable ways ransomware operators get in' (RDP #5, BlueKeep). The fail-burst+success+same-external-IP temporal correlation is the high-fidelity shape; bare 4625 counts alone are noise. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/001/ • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security/please-read-me-opportunistic-ransomware-devastating-mysql-servers
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest / red-team RDP password spray from an external range
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) performing authenticated RDP checks
  • A user fat-fingering their password several times then succeeding from a home/VPN public IP
  • Shared admin account locked out repeatedly during a legitimate maintenance window, then a correct login
  • MSP/remote-support tool reconnecting with stale cached creds before refresh
Suppression filter
| where FailedAccounts >= 2 or FailedCount >= 50   // require account-spray breadth or high burst to drop single-user fat-finger cases
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and unexpected (geo, ASN, threat-intel); pull FailedAccounts — spraying many usernames is far more suspicious than one user retrying. Check whether the successful account is privileged. 2) Contain: disable/force-reset the compromised account, kill the active RDP session, and block the source IP at the perimeter/NSG; restrict RDP to VPN/jump-host only. 3) Hunt: from that host, look for post-logon discovery, new local accounts, service installs, vssadmin shadow deletion, and lateral RDP/SMB to other internal hosts using the same credential.
let lookback = 7d;
let bruteForce = DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where LogonType == "RemoteInteractive" and ActionType == "LogonFailed" and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FailedCount = count(), FailedAccounts = dcount(AccountName), FailStart = min(Timestamp), FailEnd = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceId, RemoteIP, Hour = bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where FailedCount >= 20;   // 20 = RDP password-guessing burst floor; legit users rarely exceed ~5 fails/hr
DeviceLogonEvents

| where LogonType == "RemoteInteractive" and ActionType == "LogonSuccess" and RemoteIPType == "Public"

| where Timestamp between (FailStart .. FailEnd + 1h)
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteIP, FailedCount, FailedAccounts, FailStart, FailEnd
| order by SuccessTime desc

    by Computer, IpAddress, Hour = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where FailedCount >= 20;   // 20 = RDP password-guessing burst floor
SecurityEvent

External access to exposed phpMyAdmin / WordPress admin panel AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound web requests from the public internet to the specific admin panels the report flags as top-10 exposures — phpMyAdmin (#7) and the WordPress admin panel (#5) — surfacing the 'why is it reachable at all' panels being probed/used from outside. Article-specific because it pins the named panel URIs rather than generic admin-login activity. Rationale: Uses the article's exact named exposures (phpMyAdmin Admin Panel Exposed 8%, WordPress Admin Panel Exposed 15%) as the URI anchors and scopes to external source IPs so it surfaces panels that 'have no business being publicly reachable'. Web access logs are not in Defender XDR, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan, Censys, masscan, GreyNoise) routinely probing /wp-login.php
  • Legitimate site admins managing WordPress from a public/home IP
  • Authorized external vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) crawling the host
  • Uptime/monitoring services hitting the admin path as a health check
  • CDN/WAF health probes or bot traffic following links to wp-admin
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","nmap","masscan","zgrab","CensysInspect","Expanse") and scStatus !in ("401","403","404")   // drop known scanners and pure-probe (non-reached) requests
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the panel is supposed to be internet-facing at all (the article's core question). Check scStatus — repeated 200/302 to wp-login.php or phpMyAdmin from one external IP = successful reach; 401/403 = probing. Correlate the cIP against threat intel. 2) Contain: if the panel should not be public, restrict it to VPN/allow-list at the WAF/NSG or take it offline; if a successful auth is seen, reset the affected app/admin credentials. 3) Hunt: review the same source IP for SQLi/path-traversal payloads in csUriQuery, plugin-upload or theme-editor activity (webshell drop), and any new admin user creation in the application.
let lookback = 7d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("phpmyadmin", "wp-login", "wp-admin")
| where isnotempty(cIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))   // external clients only
| summarize Hits = count(), Paths = make_set(csUriStem, 25), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), Agents = make_set(csUserAgent, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by cIP, sSiteName, Computer
| where Hits >= 10   // repeated panel probing in window; one-off bookmark hit is benign
| order by Hits desc

PLEASE_READ_ME MySQL backdoor user 'mysqlbackups' created after DB brute-force AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step of the PLEASE_READ_ME campaign referenced in the article: after brute-forcing an internet-facing MySQL server, the operators add a backdoor account mysqlbackups'@'%' for return access. Fires on the highly specific account name in DB audit logs or in mysql-client command lines — not a generic CREATE USER. Rationale: The backdoor user mysqlbackups'@'%' is a corroborated, campaign-unique IOC (Akamai/Threatpost) not in the article text itself; matching the literal 'mysqlbackups' string in DB logs or mysql-client cmdlines is near-zero-FP and directly ties the article's PLEASE_READ_ME MySQL reference to a concrete persistence artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security/please-read-me-opportunistic-ransomware-devastating-mysql-servers • https://threatpost.com/please_read_me-ransomware-mysql-servers/162136/ • https://securityweek.com/ransomware-gang-hits-exposed-mysql-databases/
ATT&CKT1136 T1110.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DBA who genuinely named a backup service account 'mysqlbackups' (rare, verify with the team)
  • A backup/automation script string that happens to reference a mysqlbackups database object
  • Security testing or detection-validation replaying the IOC in a lab
  • Log-forwarding of historical PLEASE_READ_ME artifacts during a retro hunt
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the mysqlbackups account is not a sanctioned DBA-created account (check with the database owner); pull the source host/IP of the connection that issued the CREATE USER and whether the MySQL instance is internet-reachable. 2) Contain: DROP the mysqlbackups account, rotate all MySQL credentials, and remove the server from direct internet exposure (bind to localhost / firewall port 3306). 3) Hunt: look for preceding brute-force on 3306, the attacker's table-enumeration queries, any data export/dump, the PLEASE_READ_ME ransom-note table/row, and the same source IP touching other databases (Postgres 5432, MongoDB 27017).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "mysqlbackups"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 14d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ProcessName in~ ("mysqld", "mysql", "mariadbd", "mysqld_safe")
| where SyslogMessage has "mysqlbackups"
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)CREATE\s+USER\s+'?mysqlbackups"
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)GRANT\s+.*TO\s+'?mysqlbackups"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing host vulnerable to MongoBleed (CVE-2025-14847) memory disclosure AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces internet-exposed devices whose Defender TVM inventory flags CVE-2025-14847 (MongoBleed) — the unauthenticated MongoDB heap-memory-disclosure bug the article cites as letting attackers pull credentials and session tokens from server memory. Article-specific because it pins the exact CVE and intersects it with internet-facing posture, i.e. the exposures that are 'immediately at risk'. Rationale: Anchors on the exact pre-extracted CVE (CVE-2025-14847 / MongoBleed) corroborated by Censys, Tenable, Akamai and CISA KEV, and intersects it with DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing so it returns only the exposed-and-vulnerable MongoDB hosts the article warns are 'immediately at risk'. Posture/exposure hunt, so non-Defender SIEMs that don't ingest TVM are left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://censys.com/advisory/cve-2025-14847/ • https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2025-14847-mongobleed-mongodb-memory-leak-vulnerability-exploited-in-the-wild • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/cve-2025-14847-all-you-need-to-know-about-mongobleed
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host flagged internet-facing by Defender via an inbound rule but actually firewalled at the perimeter NSG
  • TVM lag: device already patched to a fixed MongoDB build but inventory not yet refreshed
  • Internal-only MongoDB mis-tagged as internet-facing due to a NAT/public-IP heuristic
  • Decommissioned or lab MongoDB instance kept for testing
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(RecommendedSecurityUpdate)   // drop rows where TVM already shows no outstanding update (likely patched/stale)
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the host genuinely exposes MongoDB (TCP 27017) to the internet and confirm the running version is in the vulnerable range; prioritize by data sensitivity. 2) Contain: patch to the fixed MongoDB build (or disable zlib network compression as the documented mitigation) and firewall 27017 off the public internet. 3) Hunt: because MongoBleed leaks credentials/session tokens from memory, treat any exposed instance as a possible credential-disclosure event — rotate DB and app credentials/tokens, and review MongoDB and downstream app auth logs for anomalous access following the exposure window.

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
