| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] easy-day-js dropper: node spawns detached node passing C2 host 23.254.164.123 as argv · [LLM] easy-day-js postinstall: node writes random-hex .js second-stage to OS temp dir · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] easy-day-js Mastra supply-chain C2 callback to Hostwinds 23.254.164.92 / .123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
easy-day-js Mastra supply-chain C2 callback to Hostwinds 23.254.164.92 / .123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the two hardcoded C2 hosts used by the malicious easy-day-js postinstall dropper that backdoored 140+ @mastra npm packages on 2026-06-17. 23.254.164.92:8000 serves the second-stage payload; 23.254.164.123:443 is the RAT callback. Any host reaching either IP installed a compromised @mastra package. Rationale: Both IPs are confirmed second-source by StepSecurity, Orca and JFrog write-ups of the same campaign; raw-IP IOCs on Hostwinds VPS with no legitimate business use make this a near-zero-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://orca.security/resources/blog/mastra-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1105 T1571 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher / malware analyst intentionally detonating easy-day-js in a sandbox that is still EDR-monitored
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox VM on the corporate network performing automated IOC enrichment against the IPs
  • A new tenant reusing 23.254.164.0/24 Hostwinds space for benign hosting after attacker takedown (low likelihood within the detection window)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName — expect node.exe/node spawned during an npm/pnpm/yarn install; pull the package.json / lockfile on that host for any @mastra/* or easy-day-js@1.11.22 dependency. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node process, and treat all developer/CI credentials, npm tokens, cloud keys and browser crypto-wallet extensions on that machine as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: sweep all dev/CI hosts for connections to either IP, for @mastra packages republished 2026-06-17 01:12-02:39 UTC, and for the random-hex temp .js dropper (see related UC).

easy-day-js dropper: node spawns detached node passing C2 host 23.254.164.123 as argv AIInstallation High
Detects the easy-day-js setup.cjs postinstall dropper spawning the second-stage RAT. process.execPath (node) is launched with the temp payload path plus the literal C2 host '23.254.164.123:443' as its second argument, so the C2 host appears verbatim in a process command line. This is the execution-phase pivot independent of the network connection succeeding. Rationale: The dropper code in the article passes '23.254.164.123:443' as the spawned RAT's second argument, so the C2 host is embedded verbatim in process telemetry — a guaranteed true positive that fires even if the outbound socket is firewalled. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An analyst pasting the IOC IP into a legitimate diagnostic/ping/curl command on a triage host
  • Threat-hunting or detonation tooling that references the IP in a script argument
  • Documentation or IOC-block-list deployment scripts that contain the IP string in argv
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","curl.exe","ping.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Block","deny","firewall"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is node/node.exe descending from an npm/yarn/pnpm install and that the child node was launched with a temp-dir .js path — that is the setup.cjs dropper chain, not a benign reference. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the detached node process tree, block both C2 IPs at the egress firewall, and revoke npm tokens / cloud creds present on the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host's lockfiles for easy-day-js@1.11.22 and @mastra/*@(republished 2026-06-17), and search all endpoints for the random-hex .js temp drop and connections to 23.254.164.92:8000.

| order by Timestamp desc

easy-day-js postinstall: node writes random-hex .js second-stage to OS temp dir AIInstallation Medium
Detects the file artifact of the easy-day-js dropper: setup.cjs writes the fetched second-stage payload to crypto.randomBytes(12).toString('hex') + '.js' (a 24-hex-character filename) in the OS temp directory, created by the node process running during npm install. Targets the install-time payload drop before it is executed and self-deleted. Rationale: The exact dropper code path os.tmpdir()+randomBytes(12).hex+'.js' yields a precise 24-lowercase-hex filename regex written by node — far more specific than generic 'node writes to temp', keeping FPs low while catching the artifact even after the postinstall hook self-deletes. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://orca.security/resources/blog/mastra-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tools (jest, ts-node, esbuild, webpack) that legitimately emit hashed .js scratch files to temp during CI — most use longer hashes or different extensions, but verify the writer chain
  • A developer-authored script that writes 24-hex-named .js temp files
  • Package managers caching transpiled modules under temp with hex names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","npm","pnpm","yarn")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing node process descends from an npm/pnpm/yarn install and that the file was created then deleted within seconds (dropper self-clean) — pull DeviceFileEvents FileDeleted on the same path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the temp .js if still present for IR, block C2 IPs, and rotate developer/CI secrets. 3) Hunt: correlate the file-write host against connections to 23.254.164.92:8000 / 23.254.164.123:443 and inspect lockfiles for easy-day-js@1.11.22 or @mastra packages with the 2026-06-17 republish timestamp.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has @"\Temp\" or FolderPath has "/tmp/"
| where FileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{24}\.js$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](?:Temp|tmp)[\\/][0-9a-f]{24}\.js$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: easy-day-js Dropper Writes Random-Hex JS To Temp
id: d9a3f6b8-5c41-4e7d-9a2b-1e8c4f0a6b72
description: node writes a 24-hex-character .js file into the OS temp directory during npm install - the easy-day-js setup.cjs second-stage payload drop.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/144-mastra-npm-packages-compromised-via.html
  - https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/21
tags:
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\node.exe'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Temp\'
    TargetFilename|re: '[0-9a-f]{24}\.js$'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE)) (@TargetFilename:(*\\Temp\\*.js OR *\\temp\\*.js))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/node\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/[\\\/](Temp|tmp)[\\\/][0-9a-f]{24}\.js$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") (Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*/tmp/*") by Endpoint.Filesystem.dest Endpoint.Filesystem.user Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Filesystem)`
| where match(file_name,"^[0-9a-f]{24}\.js$")
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") (Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*/tmp/*") by Endpoint.Filesystem.dest Endpoint.Filesystem.user Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Filesystem)`
| where match(file_name,"^[0-9a-f]{24}\.js$")
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123") or RemoteUrl has_any ("https://23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878", "https://23.254.164.123:443/49890878")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["https://23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878", "https://23.254.164.123:443/49890878"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176

DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48907")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48907")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound exploitation of rclone RC listener (port 5572) with inline-remote payload · [LLM] Web browser issuing requests to localhost rclone RC port 5572 (CVE-2026-49980 CSRF drive-by)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Rclone process spawning a command shell (CVE-2026-49980 RCE exploitation)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Rclone process spawning a command shell (CVE-2026-49980 RCE exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the execution outcome of CVE-2026-49980: rclone (a file-sync daemon) spawning a command interpreter or download utility as a child process. rclone has no legitimate reason to fork cmd/powershell/bash, so any such parent-child chain on a host running rcd --rc-serve is high-confidence exploitation of the unauthenticated inline-remote command-execution sink. Rationale: Uses the article's named binary (rclone) as parent and the command-execution outcome described ('execute a command as the rclone process user'). rclone forking a shell is near-zero in normal ops, making this the highest-fidelity signal of successful CVE-2026-49980 exploitation. Cross-checked against GHSA-25qr-6mpr-f7qx and CCB Belgium advisory confirming the bearer_token_command->shell sink. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-25qr-6mpr-f7qx • https://ccb.belgium.be/advisories/warning-two-critical-unauthenticated-code-execution-vulnerabilities-rclone-patch • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rclone/rclone/CVE-2026-49980/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin scripting around rclone via a wrapper that legitimately shells out (e.g. a backup script where rclone is invoked BY bash, not the reverse — check parent direction)
  • rclone rc remote-control automation invoking curl for health checks via an operator-built supervisor
  • Container entrypoints where rclone and a shell share a short-lived process tree under PID 1
  • Monitoring agents that exec rclone and then a shell sequentially under the same session (not a true parent-child)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","healthcheck")) and ProcessCommandLine !has "--version"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and rclone's own command line on the host; confirm rclone was running with rcd/--rc-serve and no --rc-user/--rc-pass. Identify the RemoteIP that hit the RC port immediately prior. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the rclone process, and block the source IP at the perimeter; rotate any credentials accessible to the rclone process user. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound connections to the rclone RC port (5572) from external IPs, search for follow-on shell activity, dropped files, and lateral movement from the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rclone.exe","rclone")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","bash.exe","bash","sh","dash","zsh","python","python3","python.exe","curl","curl.exe","wget")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/rclone"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","/bash","/sh","/dash","/python3","/curl","/wget")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rclone Process Spawning Command Shell (CVE-2026-49980 Exploitation)

status: experimental
description: Detects rclone spawning a command interpreter or download utility, indicating exploitation of CVE-2026-49980 unauthenticated command execution via inline remote instantiation in rclone rcd --rc-serve.

logsource:

detection:

      - '\rundll32.exe'

      - '/sh'

  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\rclone.exe OR *\\Rclone.exe OR *\\RCLONE.EXE) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^rclone(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32)\.exe$|\/(bash|sh|dash|zsh|python3|curl|wget)$/i

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="rclone.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="rclone") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","bash","sh","dash","python","python3","curl","wget")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="rclone.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="rclone") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","bash","sh","dash","python","python3","curl","wget")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Rclone RC server running with --rc-serve and no HTTP authentication (CVE-2026-49980 exposure) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces the exact vulnerable deployment described in the advisory: an rclone rc/rcd process launched with --rc-serve but WITHOUT --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-htpasswd. This is the precondition state that makes the host exploitable; flags it (and whether --rc-addr exposes it beyond localhost) before an attacker reaches it. Rationale: Encodes the article's explicit preconditions verbatim: --rc-serve present AND none of --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-htpasswd, with --rc-addr surfaced as the localhost-vs-network reachability differentiator. Concrete flag strings make this near-zero FP. Affected range and preconditions confirmed against the GitLab GLAD and rclone forum 1.74.3 release notes. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rclone/rclone/CVE-2026-49980/ • https://forum.rclone.org/t/rclone-release-1-74-3/53880
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate localhost-only rcd usage where --rc-addr is absent (still vulnerable to the Firefox CSRF vector, but lower priority — RemotelyReachable=false)
  • Dev/test boxes intentionally running an unauthenticated RC for local tooling
  • Ephemeral CI runners spinning up rclone rcd for a build step then tearing down
  • Internal automation that fronts rclone RC with a network ACL instead of HTTP auth (compensating control — verify firewall)
Suppression filter
| where RemotelyReachable == true
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm rclone version on the host (vulnerable if <=1.74.2) and whether --rc-addr binds to a non-loopback interface; check perimeter/host firewall for exposure of the RC port. 2) Contain: add --rc-user/--rc-pass or drop --rc-serve and restart the service, or restrict the listener to 127.0.0.1; upgrade to 1.74.3+. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (rclone spawning shells) and inbound-connection telemetry on the RC port for this host to rule out prior exploitation during the exposure window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("rclone.exe","rclone")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-serve"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--rc-user","--rc-pass","--rc-htpasswd"))
| extend RemotelyReachable = ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, RemotelyReachable, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/rclone"
| where CommandLine has "--rc-serve"
| where not(CommandLine has_any ("--rc-user","--rc-pass","--rc-htpasswd"))
| extend RemotelyReachable = CommandLine has "--rc-addr"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, RemotelyReachable
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rclone RC Server Started Without HTTP Authentication (CVE-2026-49980 Exposure)
id: 4c91f0d2-7a6e-4b3c-9e21-8d5a6b0c1f33
status: experimental
description: Detects rclone launched with --rc-serve but without --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-htpasswd, the vulnerable unauthenticated deployment state for CVE-2026-49980.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:*\\rclone.exe OR @Image:*\\Rclone.exe) @CommandLine:*\-\-rc\-serve* -@CommandLine:(*\-\-rc\-user* OR *\-\-rc\-pass* OR *\-\-rc\-htpasswd*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(\\rclone\.exe|\/rclone)$/i

| NOT (CommandLine=/--rc-(user|pass|htpasswd)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="rclone.exe" OR Processes.process_name="rclone") AND Processes.process="*--rc-serve*" AND NOT (Processes.process="*--rc-user*" OR Processes.process="*--rc-pass*" OR Processes.process="*--rc-htpasswd*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval remotely_reachable=if(like(process,"%--rc-addr%"),"yes","no") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="rclone.exe" OR Processes.process_name="rclone") AND Processes.process="*--rc-serve*" AND NOT (Processes.process="*--rc-user*" OR Processes.process="*--rc-pass*" OR Processes.process="*--rc-htpasswd*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval remotely_reachable=if(like(process,"%--rc-addr%"),"yes","no") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Inbound exploitation of rclone RC listener (port 5572) with inline-remote payload AIDelivery Medium
Detects an attacker reaching the rclone RC HTTP listener from a non-loopback source and/or GET/HEAD requests carrying inline-remote command-execution markers (bearer_token_command, global.http_proxy, inline local: backend, URL-encoded shell metacharacters). Targets the network/HTTP layer of CVE-2026-49980 — the single unauthenticated request that triggers backend init. Rationale: Pins on the rclone RC default port 5572 plus the corroborated dangerous backend option bearer_token_command and the article's named global.http_proxy / inline local: read vector, with URL-encoded shell metacharacters. Defender/Falcon catch the non-loopback reachability the article calls out (--rc-addr); Sentinel CommonSecurityLog inspects the HTTP payload at a fronting WAF/proxy. bearer_token_command sink confirmed via CVE-2026-41179 write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/cve-2026-41179 • https://ccb.belgium.be/advisories/warning-two-critical-unauthenticated-code-execution-vulnerabilities-rclone-patch • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-25qr-6mpr-f7qx
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote administration of the RC API from a jump host over an authenticated channel (still hits port 5572 from non-loopback)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualss) probing port 5572 during authorized scans
  • A monitoring system polling the rclone RC for status across the network
  • Reverse-proxy health checks that include query strings resembling config syntax — verify the source is an internal LB
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !startswith "10." and RemoteIP !startswith "192.168." and RemoteIP !startswith "172.16."
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full RequestURL for inline backend options (bearer_token_command, command=, pipe/semicolon metacharacters) and resolve the SourceIP — internal admin host vs unknown external. 2) Contain: block the source IP, restrict the RC listener to localhost or add HTTP auth, and snapshot the host for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate the connection time with UC1 (rclone spawning a shell) on the same DeviceName within seconds; if a shell fired, treat as confirmed RCE and escalate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rclone.exe","rclone")
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 5572
| where RemoteIPType != "Loopback"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, LocalPort
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 5572 or RequestURL has ":5572"
| where RequestMethod in ("GET","HEAD")
| where RequestURL has_any ("bearer_token_command","global.http_proxy","command=",":local",",exec","%7C","%26","%24","%3B","$(","|",";")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 LocalPort=5572 ContextImageFileName=/(\\rclone\.exe|\/rclone)$/i
| NOT cidr("127.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, LocalPort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=5572 AND All_Traffic.direction="inbound" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where NOT cidrmatch("127.0.0.0/8", src) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=5572 AND All_Traffic.direction="inbound" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where NOT cidrmatch("127.0.0.0/8", src) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Vulnerable rclone version present (CVE-2026-49980, 1.46.0–1.74.2) AIReconnaissance High
Exposure-management hunt that inventories hosts running an rclone build in the affected range (>=1.46.0, <=1.74.2) for CVE-2026-49980 / CVE-2026-41179, so the SOC can prioritise patching to 1.74.3+ before the RC sink is reachable. Pairs the version check with the CVE id where TVM has populated it. Rationale: Uses the exact affected version range and CVE identifiers from the advisory (confirmed against the GitLab GLAD entry and rclone 1.74.3 release notes). parse_version gives a precise range filter rather than fragile string matching. Note: rclone is often a portable binary and may not appear in TVM inventory on every host — combine with UC2 process-cmdline detection for full coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rclone/rclone/CVE-2026-49980/ • https://forum.rclone.org/t/rclone-release-1-74-3/53880
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts where rclone is present but the RC API is never enabled (vulnerable binary, not an exploitable surface) — cross-check with UC2
  • Portable rclone.exe copies dropped in user profiles that TVM may double-count
  • Air-gapped or firewalled hosts where the RC listener is unreachable (lower priority)
  • Vendored rclone embedded inside a third-party backup appliance reported under the appliance's software name
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is within 1.46.0–1.74.2 and check whether the host actually runs rcd/--rc-serve (join to UC2 results). 2) Contain: schedule upgrade to rclone 1.74.3+ for confirmed-running instances first; for non-running binaries, remove or update during the next window. 3) Hunt: for any host that was both vulnerable AND running an unauthenticated RC, retro-hunt UC1/UC3 over the exposure period to confirm no prior exploitation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "rclone"
| extend Ver = parse_version(SoftwareVersion)
| where Ver >= parse_version("1.46.0") and Ver <= parse_version("1.74.2")
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-49980","CVE-2026-41179") or SoftwareName has "rclone"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
Web browser issuing requests to localhost rclone RC port 5572 (CVE-2026-49980 CSRF drive-by) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the browser-driven exploitation multiplier the advisory describes: a public HTTPS page with an <img> tag pointing at http://127.0.0.1:5572/... causes a local browser (Firefox in testing) to trigger the rclone RC payload against a localhost-only listener. Hunts browsers making connections to loopback:5572. Rationale: Directly implements the article's 'Additional impact' note: Firefox triggering the payload from a public page via an <img> pointing at http://127.0.0.1:5572. The browser-to-loopback:5572 pair is the unique signature of this CSRF vector and is not normal browser behaviour. sentinel_kql left empty: Sentinel has no clean table joining process image to a loopback network connection (Sysmon EID 3 lands in WindowsEvent/Event without parsed process+dest fields in this tenant). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qw24-gh76-8rvv • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-25qr-6mpr-f7qx
ATT&CKT1190 T1189
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running rclone rcd locally and using the rclone Web GUI (which the browser legitimately loads from 127.0.0.1:5572)
  • Browser extensions or local dev tools that probe localhost ports for service discovery
  • A user intentionally browsing to the rclone RC web interface
  • Security tooling that scans localhost ports from a browser-based scanner
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--app=http://127.0.0.1:5572" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "localhost:5572"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the page/tab that initiated the connection (browser history around the Timestamp) and whether the user runs a local rclone rcd; inspect any subsequent rclone child-process activity. 2) Contain: if the user is not an intentional rclone RC operator, treat as drive-by — isolate, capture browser history, and bind the rclone listener to require auth or stop it. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 on the same host for rclone-spawned shells, and review web proxy logs for the external page hosting the malicious <img> reference.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| where RemotePort == 5572
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or RemoteIPType == "Loopback"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| where RemotePort == 5572
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or RemoteIPType == "Loopback"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiteLLM CVE-2026-49468: Host header injection on protected management routes AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to LiteLLM management routes (/key, /user, /team, /model, /customer, /spend, /organization) where the Host header carries path/route tokens or control characters. CVE-2026-49468 abuses Starlette reconstructing request.url.path from the Host header, so an attacker injects route fragments into Host to make the auth gate evaluate a different route than FastAPI dispatched. Rationale: Uses the exact LiteLLM management-route prefixes (corroborated via DeepWiki/docs) plus the article's stated root cause — Host header reconstructed into request.url.path — to flag Host values carrying path/route tokens or control chars, the literal injection mechanism. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: this is an HTTP-header detection on a FastAPI web app; those telemetry sources carry no Host-header/route semantics. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/ • https://gbhackers.com/critical-litellm-flaw/ • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy
ATT&CKT1190 T1036
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate reverse proxy/CDN appending X-Forwarded host data into a single Host field
  • Load balancer health-check probes using IP:port style Host values
  • Misconfigured client libraries sending full URLs as the Host header
  • Internal API gateway that rewrites Host with a routing prefix
  • Pentest/vuln-scanner activity from an authorized assessment
Suppression filter
| where not(HostHdr matches regex @"^[a-zA-Z0-9._\-]+(:\d{1,5})?$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request line for the flagged events — confirm the Host header genuinely contains route tokens or control chars (not just an odd-but-legit FQDN) and note the HTTP status returned. 2) Contain: if the proxy is directly internet-reachable, place it behind a CDN/WAF or reverse proxy with a server_name allowlist (per advisory workaround) and confirm/upgrade LiteLLM to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: from the same SrcIpAddr, pivot to all management-route requests, check for 200/201 responses and any /key/generate or /user/new actions that would indicate created keys or accounts to revoke.
let mgmt = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| extend HostHdr = tostring(HttpHostName)
| where isnotempty(HostHdr)
// CVE-2026-49468: Host header is reconstructed into request.url.path; injection puts route tokens / control chars in Host
| where HostHdr matches regex @"[/\\;@]" or HostHdr has_any ("/key","/user","/team","/model","/customer","/spend","/organization","..","%2e")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HostHdr, HttpMethod, Url, StatusCode = toint(HttpStatusCode), HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiteLLM auth-bypass success: 401/403 then 200 to same management route (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation High
Correlates failed auth (401/403) followed within 5 minutes by a successful (200/201/204) response to a LiteLLM management route from the same source. A fail-then-succeed sequence against protected /key, /user, /team, /model routes is the signature of a working Host-header auth bypass, especially when the Host header value changes between the two requests. Rationale: Targets the article's core impact (unauthenticated access to protected management routes) via a high-fidelity temporal shape: a rejected request immediately followed by a success on the same route/source, with Host-header divergence surfaced as the injection tell. Correlation + threshold means no Sigma; HTTP-only signal means Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch cannot express it. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://gbhackers.com/critical-litellm-flaw/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/litellm/CVE-2026-49468/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin who mistyped/expired an API key, then retried with a valid one within 5 minutes
  • Token-refresh races where a client retries after a 401 with a renewed bearer token
  • Automation rotating keys that briefly 401s then succeeds
  • Load-balanced retries where the first node returns 401 due to cache lag
  • Authorized pentest replaying requests against the management API
Suppression filter
| where HostChanged == true or not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the matched pair — was the 200 served to a request lacking valid credentials, and did the Host header change between the 401 and the 200? A Host change is strong evidence of bypass. 2) Contain: block the SrcIpAddr at the WAF/proxy, force LiteLLM behind a Host-validating upstream, and upgrade to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate every management action that source performed after the success (key/user/team creation, model changes); rotate any keys created or exposed and review /spend and /user/list pulls for data access.
let win = 5m;
let mgmt = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
let fails = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (401, 403)
| project FailTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, FailUrl = Url, FailHost = tostring(HttpHostName);
let success = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (200, 201, 204)
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SuccessUrl = Url, SuccessHost = tostring(HttpHostName), HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent;
fails
| join kind=inner success on SrcIpAddr
| where SuccessTime between (FailTime .. FailTime + win)
| extend HostChanged = FailHost != SuccessHost
| project FailTime, SuccessTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SuccessTime, FailTime), SrcIpAddr, FailUrl, SuccessUrl, FailHost, SuccessHost, HostChanged, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by SuccessTime desc

LiteLLM rapid enumeration across multiple management-route categories (CVE-2026-49468) AIReconnaissance Medium
Flags a single source that successfully (200/201/204) hits 3+ distinct LiteLLM management-route categories (key/user/team/model/customer/spend/organization) within 10 minutes. Post-bypass exploitation of CVE-2026-49468 typically fans out across the management surface; legitimate admin activity usually stays within a narrow subset of routes. Rationale: Builds on the advisory's enumerated management surface (>14 routes across 7 categories, confirmed via LiteLLM DeepWiki) and treats breadth-of-access as the anomaly signal post-bypass. Threshold aggregation rules out Sigma; HTTP-route semantics rule out Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy • https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/public_routes
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LiteLLM admin UI page load that fans out across several management endpoints in one session
  • Infrastructure-as-code/Terraform reconciliation touching keys, users, teams and models
  • Scheduled reporting job pulling /spend, /user/list and /key/list together
  • Onboarding automation that provisions a team, users and keys in sequence
  • Backup/export tooling iterating the full management API
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the source is the admin UI/IaC service account (expected) or an unrecognized/external IP; check whether the requests carried valid auth. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, block the source and restrict the proxy to internal networks plus a Host-validating upstream, then upgrade to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: review state-changing calls in the burst (/key/generate, /user/new, /team/new, /model/new) and revoke artifacts created; correlate the same SrcIpAddr against the 401-then-200 detection to confirm bypass.
let mgmt = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (200, 201, 204)
| extend Category = extract(@"/(key|user|team|model|customer|spend|organization)/", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(Category)
| summarize Categories = make_set(Category), CategoryCount = dcount(Category), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hosts = make_set(HttpHostName, 10) by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CategoryCount >= 3   // 3+ distinct management categories in 10m = enumeration, not normal admin
| order by LastSeen desc

LiteLLM successful management-route access from external/unauthenticated source (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful (200/201/204) access to LiteLLM management routes that either carried no Authorization header or originated from a public (non-RFC1918) source IP. CVE-2026-49468 only works where the proxy is directly reachable without an upstream Host validator, so externally-sourced or credential-less successes on /key, /user, /team, /model routes are the direct expression of the bypass impact. Rationale: Encodes the advisory's central impact ("unauthenticated access to protected management routes") and its precondition (proxy directly reachable / no Host-normalizing upstream) using credential-less or public-source successes on the confirmed management routes. Higher FP rate where admins legitimately reach the API over the internet — pairs best with the 401-then-200 and enumeration UCs. HTTP-only signal, so Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch are empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/ • https://www.cryptika.com/critical-litellm-flaw-allows-authentication-bypass-via-host-header-injection/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin managing keys/users from a home or office public IP
  • CI/CD or SaaS automation calling the management API from a cloud egress IP
  • Logging pipeline that strips the Authorization header before forwarding (false 'no auth')
  • Monitoring/health checkers hitting management routes from external probes
  • Partner integration provisioning keys over the public internet
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog","Pingdom","UptimeRobot","GoogleHC")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is genuinely external/unexpected and that the 200 was served without valid credentials (account for log pipelines that drop the Authorization header). 2) Contain: place the proxy behind a CDN/WAF or reverse proxy with server_name allowlists, or restrict the listener to internal networks, and upgrade to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate all management actions from that source, rotate any keys returned by /key/generate or /key/info, audit /user/new and /team/new for rogue accounts, and review /spend output for data exposure.
let mgmt = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (200, 201, 204)
// successful management access with no Authorization header OR from a public (non-RFC1918) source
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) or (isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, IsPublic = iff(isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)), true, false), HasAuthHeader = isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization), HttpMethod, Url, HostHdr = tostring(HttpHostName), StatusCode = toint(HttpStatusCode), HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — A Forgotten Contributor Account Compromised the Entire Mastra npm Package Scope
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm install pulls malicious easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs + .pkg marker files) · [LLM] easy-day-js stealer persistence masquerading as Node tooling (NodePackages / LaunchAgent / systemd) · [LLM] Mastra easy-day-js second-stage stealer payload by SHA256 · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Cross-platform stealer RAT C2 beacon to 23.254.164.123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
npm install pulls malicious easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs + .pkg marker files) AIInstallation High
Hunts a build/dev host resolving the trojanized easy-day-js dependency: the package landing under node_modules\easy-day-js, its setup.cjs postinstall dropper, and the ~/.pkg_history / ~/.pkg_logs marker files the dropper writes to track installs. Article-specific because these exact filenames and the easy-day-js package path are the carrier injected into the @mastra scope. Rationale: Anchors on the exact carrier filenames named by Snyk and corroborated by Microsoft/StepSecurity: the easy-day-js node_modules path, setup.cjs postinstall dropper, and the .pkg_history/.pkg_logs markers — none of which exist on a clean host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • Defenders deliberately caching the malicious tarball for IR/forensics
  • A renamed-but-unrelated package legitimately named easy-day-js in an internal registry mirror (rare)
  • Backup/EDR agents re-scanning an already-quarantined node_modules tree
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host resolved easy-day-js@1.11.21/1.11.22 — check the project lockfile and whether npm install ran on/after 2026-06-17; pull the SHA256 of any setup.cjs found. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node-spawned detached process, and treat it as credential+wallet exposure — force-reset npm tokens, cloud creds, and browser-stored secrets used on that host; revoke/rotate any wallet seed phrases. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for outbound connections to 23.254.164.92/.123 and persistence under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages; sweep CI runners and other dev laptops sharing the lockfile.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("setup.cjs",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")) or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.cjs",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs") or TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node dropper fetches second stage from Hostwinds raw IP 23.254.164.92:8000 AIDelivery High
Hunts the easy-day-js dropper's second-stage download: an outbound connection to the hardcoded Hostwinds host 23.254.164.92 on port 8000 (https://23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878), typically initiated by node.exe after TLS verification is disabled. High-fidelity because the IP+port are dedicated attacker infrastructure confirmed by multiple vendors. Rationale: Uses the verbatim dropper URL host/port (23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878) from the article; Microsoft and StepSecurity independently list this as the stage-2 download endpoint, so a hit is near-certainly the dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js
ATT&CKT1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation of the sample making the same fetch
  • A blue-team connectivity test confirming the IOC is reachable/blocked
  • Shared NAT egress where another tool coincidentally targets the same /24 (verify exact IP+port)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess — a node.exe/npm child reaching this IP confirms dropper execution; capture the host, user, and the resolved second-stage file in %TEMP%. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.92 at the egress firewall, isolate the host, and treat as credential+wallet compromise (rotate dev/cloud/npm tokens, browser secrets). 3) Hunt: from the same host pivot to 23.254.164.123 beacons and C:\ProgramData\NodePackages persistence; block the full 23.254.164.0/24 Hostwinds range pending review.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.254.164.92" and RemotePort == 8000
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "23.254.164.92" and DstPortNumber == 8000
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cross-platform stealer RAT C2 beacon to 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the second-stage crypto-stealer/RAT beaconing to its C2 at 23.254.164.123 roughly every 10 minutes over a self-signed wolfSSL channel. Aggregates repeat connections per host to surface the sustained beacon cadence rather than a single hit, distinguishing it from the one-shot dropper download. Rationale: Anchors on the article's RAT C2 IP (23.254.164.123) and the ~10-minute beacon described; the count>=3 aggregation captures the sustained cadence and filters single stray probes. No Sigma emitted because the detection is a threshold/aggregation, not a single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.mend.io/blog/mastra-npm-scope-takeover-easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/IR detonation of the stealer producing repeat beacons
  • Security tooling actively probing the IOC for reachability
  • Another host in the same /24 being contacted for unrelated reasons (pin to exact IP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm beacon cadence and the originating process; a ~10-min periodic connection from a non-browser process is the RAT. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 23.254.164.123 at egress, and snapshot memory before reimage; treat all secrets entered on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: enumerate persistence (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages on Windows, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.nvm.protocal.plist on macOS, ~/.config/systemd/user/nvmconf.service on Linux) and check other hosts beaconing to the same /24.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.254.164.123"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), BeaconHours=dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1h)),
            FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
            Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 5), Proc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName)
            by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where ConnCount >= 3   // >=3 hits = repeat beacon, not a stray probe
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "23.254.164.123"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), BeaconHours=dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)),
            FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated),
            Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber, 5) by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr
| where ConnCount >= 3   // >=3 hits = repeat beacon, not a stray probe
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:23.254.164.123
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="23.254.164.123"
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| count >= 3
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count dc(_time) as distinct_times min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="23.254.164.123" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(_time) as distinct_times min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="23.254.164.123" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
easy-day-js stealer persistence masquerading as Node tooling (NodePackages / LaunchAgent / systemd) AIInstallation High
Hunts the cross-platform persistence the stealer installs while disguised as Node tooling: Windows staging under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, macOS LaunchAgent com.nvm.protocal.plist, and Linux systemd user service nvmconf.service. Article-specific because these exact persistence names are unique to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three campaign-unique persistence names from the article (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, com.nvm.protocal.plist, nvmconf.service) — the misspelled 'protocal' and 'nvmconf' are distinctive enough that a hit is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-iocs-and-response-runbook
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally writing to C:\ProgramData\NodePackages (verify against the exact plist/service names)
  • Restored backup re-creating a previously-quarantined persistence file
  • IR responder copying the artifact for analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the persistence file content points to a NodePackages-staged payload or beacon; capture the writing process. 2) Contain: remove the LaunchAgent/systemd unit/Run entry, kill the persisted process, isolate the host, and rotate all credentials/wallets used there. 3) Hunt: correlate with 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and the easy-day-js install artifacts on the same and peer hosts; sweep all OS types since persistence is cross-platform.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages" or TargetFileName in~ ("com.nvm.protocal.plist","nvmconf.service")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra easy-day-js second-stage stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the obfuscated cross-platform crypto-stealer/RAT second stage by file hash on both write and execution. Hash matching is resilient to IP/infra rotation and is effectively zero-FP; the primary hash (221c45...) is the article-named stage-2 payload corroborated by Microsoft. Rationale: Primary hash 221c45a7... is the article-named second-stage payload and is corroborated by Microsoft Threat Intelligence; the additional campaign hashes are bundled IOCs. Hash matching is zero-FP and survives infrastructure rotation, complementing the IP-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/sandbox host where the sample was intentionally executed
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy retaining the hash on disk
  • Threat-intel platform caching the sample for enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: any hit is high-confidence malicious — confirm host, user, and whether the hash was written vs executed; the payload self-deletes, so a FileWrite without a later process may indicate cleanup. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory, and treat as full credential+wallet compromise — rotate cloud/npm/dev secrets and assume browser-stored wallet data exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and NodePackages/LaunchAgent/systemd persistence; submit the hash to org-wide retro-hunt across EDR.

  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="FileWrite", Path=FolderPath, Name=FileName, SHA256,

( DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (payloadHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="ProcExec", Path=FolderPath, Name=FileName, SHA256,
            Proc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine )
| order by Timestamp desc
